products.title: Micranthemum Glomeratus (Pearl Weed)
products.body_html:
Want one plant that can be a carpet or a hedge? Pearl Weed does both — trimmed low it creeps sideways into a fine bright-green mat, left alone it grows upright into a bushy column. Few plants change role that completely depending on how you cut them.

You may know it as Micranthemum micranthemoides or Hemianthus micranthemoides. Those are the same plant — see the note below.

What You’ll Receive

Enhance your aquascape with our premium-quality Micranthemum glomeratus, available in three flexible planting formats:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approx. 6+ unrooted, loose fresh-cut stems – flexible for custom layout
  • Fresh-Cut Bunched: Approx. 6+ unrooted stems bundled with foam and plant weight for easy placement
  • Fresh-Cut Potted: Approx. 6+ unrooted stems securely potted in a net pot with rockwool for stable growth

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pearl Weed, also known as Pearl Grass, Baby Tears
  • Scientific name — Micranthemum glomeratus
  • Also known as — Micranthemum micranthemoides, Hemianthus micranthemoides (both outdated)
  • Origin — Florida
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6+ fresh-cut stems, roughly 2-4 in
  • Mature height — 2–4 in trimmed, taller left upright
  • Suits — 5 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Why two scientific names?

Pearl Weed was sold for decades as Micranthemum micranthemoides (also written Hemianthus micranthemoides), and most aquarists still know it by those names.

Micranthemum micranthemoides was a real species from the tidal river margins of the eastern United States. It has not been recorded in the wild since the 1940s and is considered extinct. The plant circulating in the hobby under that label was correctly identified in 2011 as a different, living species — Micranthemum glomeratus, from Florida.

So the plant you receive is Micranthemum glomeratus: the same Pearl Weed you have always bought, correctly named.

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium. More light gives tighter, denser growth
  • CO₂ — Not required. It carpets faster with it, but does not need it
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient substrate makes a visible difference
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed in paludariums
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Trimming decides what plant you get. Cut it back repeatedly and it branches sideways into a carpet. Leave it and it climbs into a soft green bush. Decide which you want before planting, because the two need different spacing.
  • Don't bury the stems deeply. They are fine and rot if pushed too far into substrate — plant just enough to hold them.
  • Replant the trimmings. Cut tops root readily at the nodes, so one portion fills a foreground over a couple of months at no extra cost.
  • In a nano tank its tiny leaves work as a background filler as well as a carpet — unusual flexibility for a single species.

Prefer the sterile format? See Pearl Weed Vitro Culture, free of snails and algae.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Micranthemum Care Guide.

Notes

  • Images shown are sample representations only. Live plants may vary in size, colour, and form based on growing conditions. Unless stated otherwise, plants may arrive in emersed form and are not guaranteed to be pest- or pesticide-free.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

This plant is ideal for creating dense group plantings and can be used in various aquascaping styles.

products.title: Salvinia Minima
products.body_html:
Need nitrate gone and algae starved out fast? Salvinia Minima does it quicker than almost anything. Small quilted leaves with water-repellent hairs spread across the surface, soaking up nutrients and shading the tank below — and it grows fast enough that thinning it becomes a weekly job.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a small portion
  • Approx. 2" x 2" in size

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Salvinia Minima, Water Spangles
  • Scientific name — Salvinia minima
  • Plant type — Floating fern
  • Placement — Floating on the surface
  • Mature height — 0.5–1 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner. Close to unkillable
  • Light — Medium to high, though it manages on less
  • CO₂ — Not required! It takes carbon straight from the air
  • Water — 65–85°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Feeding — Water column
  • Propagation — Runners; it multiplies on its own

Grower’s Notes

  • Thin it every week. This is the fastest-spreading plant we sell, and left alone it forms a solid mat that shades out everything beneath it.
  • The leaf hairs repel water, so it tolerates surface movement far better than Red Root Floater or Frogbit — a good choice if your filter breaks the surface.
  • Yellowing usually means iron or micronutrients. Floating plants feed entirely from the water column and show a deficiency before rooted plants do.
  • Bigger sister plant: if you want the same look at three times the leaf size, see Salvinia Natans.

Notes

  • Cannot ship to Texas. Salvinia minima is listed as an invasive species there — please do not order if you are in Texas.
  • Photos are for reference; portion size and leaf density vary with growing conditions.
  • Never release aquatic plants into natural waterways. This species spreads rapidly and can do real damage to local ecosystems.

products.title: Dracaena Sanderiana – Lucky Bamboo
products.body_html:
🎋 Dracaena sanderiana – Lucky Bamboo
Semi-Aquatic Ornamental Plant | Can Grow in Aquariums with Emerged Foliage

Dracaena sanderiana, widely known as Lucky Bamboo, is a beautiful and resilient ornamental plant often used in aquariums, paludariums, and indoor decorative displays. Despite its common name, Lucky Bamboo is not a true bamboo but a member of the Dracaena family. Its smooth green stems and elegant narrow leaves create a clean, minimal aesthetic that pairs beautifully with modern aquascapes and indoor plant arrangements.

One unique feature of Dracaena sanderiana is that the stem can safely grow in aquarium water, making it popular for aquarists who want a plant that bridges both aquatic and terrestrial environments. The stems tolerate full submersion, but the leaves are not adapted for underwater life.

When fully submerged, the leaves will typically decline and melt after a short period of time. For long-term health, the leaves should grow above the water line, where they will continue to develop normally and can thrive permanently in that position. This makes Lucky Bamboo ideal for aquariums where the stem is placed in water while the foliage grows above the tank.

🌟 Key Features

Scientific Name: Dracaena sanderiana
Common Name: Lucky Bamboo
Plant Type: Semi-aquatic ornamental houseplant

• Aquarium Compatible Stem: The stem can grow submerged in aquarium water.
• Emergent Growth Habit: Leaves must grow above the water surface for long-term health.
• Elegant Upright Structure: Smooth green stalks with narrow pointed leaves create a clean decorative look.
• Versatile Placement: Perfect for aquariums, paludariums, ripariums, and indoor plant displays.

🌱 Growth & Care

Lighting: Low to moderate light
Water Parameters: Adaptable to most aquarium conditions
Placement: Stem can be placed underwater, but leaves must remain above water
Growth Form: Upright stem plant with emergent foliage

Important:
While the stem tolerates submersion, the leaves will only survive a short time underwater. For permanent growth in an aquarium environment, position the plant so that the foliage grows above the water line.

🪴 Aquarium & Decorative Benefits

• Natural Aquascape Accent: Adds vertical structure and a natural look to aquariums.
• Perfect for Open-Top Tanks: Ideal for aquariums where plants can grow above the water surface.
• Low Maintenance: Hardy and adaptable, making it suitable for beginners and experienced hobbyists alike.

📦 What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Dracaena sanderiana (Lucky Bamboo) carefully prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®:

Fresh Cut Plant:
• 1 healthy stem cutting approximately 8–12 inches tall with attached leaves.

⚠️ Care Disclaimer

Dracaena sanderiana is commonly used in aquariums, but only the stem should remain submerged.
Leaves are not aquatic and will not survive permanently underwater.

For best long-term results, position the plant so the stem grows in water while the leaves grow above the aquarium.

🚫 State Restrictions Notice ♻️ Be a Responsible Aquatic Plants Owner

Certain aquatic plants may be restricted or regulated in some U.S. states. Always check your local and state regulations before purchasing or introducing plants into natural waterways. Never release aquarium plants into the wild.

products.title: American Frogbit
products.body_html:
Miniature lily pads that need no planting. Limnobium spongia — American Frogbit — floats round, glossy leaves on the surface with a curtain of fine roots trailing beneath. Native to North America, undemanding, and one of the few floaters that looks deliberate rather than weedy.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as a small portion – approx. 1–2 individual plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — American Frogbit
  • Scientific name — Limnobium spongia
  • Origin — North America
  • Placement — Free-floating on the surface
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required. It takes CO₂ from the air
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed on wet margins
  • Propagation — Runners — daughter plants form on side stolons

Grower’s Notes

  • Keep the leaves dry on top. Frogbit hates water landing on its leaves — condensation from a tight lid or spray from a filter return makes the tops rot. An open top or a small gap under the lid solves it, and it's the single most common reason Frogbit fails.
  • The long root curtain is the point. It gives shrimp and fry cover and pulls nutrients straight out of the water column.
  • Surface flow packs it into corners. Aim filter returns downward or add a floating ring.
  • Thin it regularly — daughter plants form fast and a sealed surface starves plants below of light.
  • Compare with Amazon Frogbit: similar habit, larger leaves, tropical rather than North American.

Notes

  • As a floating plant, American Frogbit may spread quickly in nutrient-rich water. Regular thinning may be required to maintain light penetration for plants below.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

featured_image.alt: Small portion of American Frogbit, 1–2 plants, ready for aquarium or pond use

products.title: Bolbitis Heudelotii (African Water Fern)
products.body_html:
Want a fern with real texture? Bolbitis heudelotii grows finely divided, almost translucent dark green fronds with a hammered surface — nothing else in a planted tank looks like it. It attaches to wood and stone rather than rooting in substrate, and it thrives in the kind of current most plants dislike.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as Bare-root plants, or Potted plants
  • Bare-root plants | approx. 6 leaf, bare-root, loose rhizome
  • Potted plants | approx. 6 leaf plant potted with rockwool and plastic net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — African Water Fern, Congo Fern
  • Scientific name — Bolbitis heudelotii
  • Origin — Tropical West and Central Africa
  • Placement — Midground to background, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 8–14 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light means algae on slow-growing fronds
  • CO₂ — Not required. It speeds growth but changes nothing else
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape and feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed in paludariums
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower’s Notes

  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie or glue it to wood or stone with the rhizome fully exposed — buried in substrate it rots, and this is the usual way Bolbitis is lost.
  • Give it flow. This is a rheophyte from fast-running African streams, and it does visibly better in current than in still water. Placing it in the outflow path is one of the few reliable ways to speed it up.
  • It is genuinely slow. Expect a month or more before the first new frond appears, and do not move it while it settles — Bolbitis resents relocation more than most epiphytes.
  • Cooler suits it. At the top of its range growth slows further and fronds are more prone to browning at the edges.
  • Divide by cutting the rhizome with a blade, leaving several fronds and some root on each section.

New to attaching plants? Read our guide on how to attach epiphyte plants to driftwood and rock.

Notes

  • Pictures are not the actual plants you will receive, but a sample representation. Frond size and colour vary with lighting, flow and nutrients.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Cardamine Lyrata
products.body_html:
A stem plant that behaves like a vine. Cardamine lyrata — Japanese Cress — carries small, round, ivy-like leaves on long trailing stems that creep across hardscape or climb toward the surface rather than standing upright. It also prefers cooler water than most tropical stems.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a Small Bare-root Plants, Bunched plants, or Potted plants
  • Small bare-root | small rooted develop plants
  • Bunched plants | rooted plants bundle with foam, and plant weight
  • Potted plants | rooted developed plants potted with net pot and rock wool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Cardamine
  • Scientific name — Cardamine lyrata
  • Also known as — Japanese Cress, Chinese Ivy
  • Origin — East Asia
  • Placement — Midground; also trails over hardscape
  • Mature height — 4–10 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 65–75°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Note the ceiling — this is a cool-water species
  • Substrate — Not required, though a nutrient substrate gives fuller growth
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed in humid terrariums
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem sections

Grower’s Notes

  • Keep it under 75°F. Cardamine comes from temperate East Asia and thins out badly in a warm tropical tank. It suits room-temperature, lightly heated and coldwater setups — which is where most of its competition won't grow.
  • Train it rather than plant it. Laid across wood or stone the stems creep and root as they go, giving a draped effect no upright stem plant produces.
  • It arrives in emersed nursery form with round leaves. Submerged growth comes in a slightly different shape — that's the plant adapting, not a mislabel.
  • Trim and replant cuttings; sections root readily from any node.
  • Fast growth means regular trimming, or it reaches the surface and shades what's below.

Notes

  • Cardamine lyrata ships in its emersed nursery form with round leaves. Once submerged, leaf shape may change and adapt to aquarium conditions. Some initial melting or leaf loss may occur during transition but new submerged growth will follow.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

featured_image.alt: Cardamine Lyrata thrives in various water conditions and adapts well to different lighting setups. It prefers moderate to high lighting and benefits from CO2 supplementation, although it can grow in low-tech setups as well. This plant is perfect for both beginner and experienced aquarists.

products.title: Ludwigia Glandulosa (Peruensis) Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Ludwigia glandulosa (Peruensis) in Vitro Culture® – Deep Red Rosette-Forming Stem Plant for Striking Aquascapes

Ludwigia glandulosa, also known as Ludwigia peruensis, is a show-stopping aquarium stem plant prized for its dramatic burgundy to deep red foliage and bold vertical structure. Native to North America, this species is widely used in Dutch-style and color-themed aquascapes where rich contrast and vibrant tones are essential. Its broad, pointed leaves and upright, bushy habit make it perfect for midground to background placement, creating a vivid focal point in any planted aquarium.

Now available in our Vitro Culture® 4-inch sterile bag, this tissue-cultured form yields approximately 3–4 small plantlets, grown in vitamin-enriched gel or liquid. Carefully propagated under sterile conditions, these plants are 100% free of snails, algae, and harmful pathogens, ensuring a safe and healthy start for even the most sensitive aquatic setups.

🌿 Key Features:

  • Scientific Name: Ludwigia glandulosa

  • Also Known As: Ludwigia peruensis

  • Leaf Color: Deep green to rich red or burgundy (depending on lighting)

  • Growth Habit: Upright rosette-like stem plant

  • Vitro Culture® Format: 4-inch sterile bag with 3–4 healthy plantlets

  • Placement: Midground to background

  • Growth Rate: Moderate

  • Difficulty Level: Moderate – requires stable, enriched conditions

💧 Optimal Growing Conditions:

  • Lighting: Medium to high (required for red pigmentation)

  • CO₂: Recommended for rich coloration and healthy growth

  • Substrate: Nutrient-rich substrate or supplemented with root tabs

  • Water Parameters: pH 6.0–7.2 | Temperature: 72–82°F (22–28°C)

  • Fertilization: Regular dosing of macro and micronutrients advised

🧪 Vitro Culture® Advantages:

  • 100% Pest-Free: No snails, algae, or chemical residues

  • Sterile & Safe: Perfect for shrimp tanks and sensitive aquascapes

  • Long Shelf Life: Store under gentle light until ready to plant

  • Easy to Plant: Rinse, separate, and insert directly into the substrate

🐠 Aquascaping Benefits:

  • High-Impact Color: Adds bold red tones that contrast beautifully with green or white plants

  • Structural Accent: Ideal for creating vertical depth in aquascapes

  • Mid-to-Back Placement: Fills space while drawing the eye upward

  • Low Maintenance: Once established, grows steadily with minimal trimming

📦 What You’ll Receive:

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing 3–4 Ludwigia glandulosa (Peruensis) plantlets, ready for rinsing, acclimation, and planting in your aquascape.

Images shown are for reference. Plant size and coloration may vary based on lighting, nutrient levels, and tank maturity. Transition from emersed to submerged form may involve slight melting before regrowth.

products.title: Vallisneria Americana
products.body_html:
Want Vallisneria that won't take over the tank? Corkscrew Val stays 8 to 12 inches instead of running to the surface, and twists its blades along their whole length into tight spirals. Of our three twisted Vals, this is the one with the widest blade — the spirals read boldly rather than as fine threads.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as loose fresh-cut plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Bare-root Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual loose, bare-root plants
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Corkscrew Val, also known as Twisted Val
  • Scientific name — Vallisneria americana 'Asiatica'
  • Origin — Asia (this cultivar); the species is North American
  • Placement — Midground, or foreground in a large tank
  • Shipped size — Approx. 2-3 bare-root plants, roughly 4-8 in
  • Mature height — 8–12 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Brighter light tightens the spiral
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–8.0. Tolerates hard, alkaline water well
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Wide blades, mid height. Jungle Val and spiralis keep growing until they hit the surface and trail along it. 'Asiatica' tops out around a foot, which is why it works where taller Vallisneria would swamp the layout.
  • Plant the crown at the substrate line, never below it. A buried crown rots — the usual reason a new Val fails in the first fortnight.
  • Feed at the roots. In inert gravel it survives but barely spreads; root tabs are what turn three plants into a colony.
  • Don't trim the tops to control height. Cut Val leaves brown at the cut and stay that way. Remove whole leaves at the base instead.
  • Runners travel fast. Pull unwanted plantlets by hand rather than cutting, and expect to thin it every month or two once established.

Choosing between our twisted Vallisneria

  • Vallisneria torta — shortest, 4–8 in. Foreground, midground and nano tanks.
  • Vallisneria americana 'Asiatica' (this plant) — 8–12 in, with a wider twisted blade.
  • Vallisneria 'Contortionist' — 10–20 in, with a narrower twisted blade. Background.

Want the tall straight-leaved version instead? See Vallisneria Spiralis (Jungle Val), which reaches 20–36 in.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Vallisneria Care Guide.

Notes

  • Leaf twist intensity and colouration may vary slightly depending on lighting and nutrients. Some initial melting is normal upon introduction. Stable conditions promote quick propagation and healthy regrowth.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Echinodorus Marble Queen
products.body_html:
Broad leaves marbled in cream and green. Echinodorus 'Marble Queen' is the variegated sword — pattern rather than colour, on a plant large enough to hold the middle of a tank. Easier than most variegated aquatics, because the cream is marbling rather than a full loss of chlorophyll.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose bare-root plants, rooted bunched, or rooted potted plants:

  • Loose Bare-Root Plants: Approximately 1–2 loose, bare-root plants for flexible planting.
  • Rooted Bunched: Approximately 1–2 plants, bundled with foam and a plant weight.
  • Rooted Potted: Approximately 1–2 plants, potted in rock wool and a net pot for secure placement.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Marble Queen Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus 'Marble Queen'
  • Also known as — Echinodorus cordifolius 'Marble Queen', Marble Queen Amazon Sword
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the genus is native to the Americas
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner, provided you feed the roots
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — root tabs or aquasoil under the crown.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette; also grows emersed, so it suits paludariums
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on aerial floral stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Variegation is marbling, not albinism. The cream areas sit in a mostly green leaf, so unlike the heavily white Anubias this plant still photosynthesises normally and stays a beginner plant. What it will do under thin light is revert — push plainer green leaves — rather than decline.
  • Feed it at the roots. Swords take nearly all their nutrition from the substrate. In inert gravel with liquid dosing alone the plant stalls and the pattern washes out, which people misread as a difficult plant rather than a hungry one.
  • Plant the crown at substrate level, never below. Cover the roots and leave the growing point exposed. A buried crown rots from the centre.
  • It propagates from floral stalks, not runners. A settled plant sends up a tall stalk carrying plantlets. Leave each attached until it has four or five leaves and its own roots, then cut it free.
  • Expect the first leaves to melt. Grown emersed, so the arriving foliage dies back as it converts. The second flush is the one that shows the marbling properly.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Amazon Sword (Echinodorus) Care Guide.

Notes

Like all Amazon Swords, the Marble Queen may undergo a brief adjustment period after planting. Some leaves may melt back, but healthy roots will quickly sprout new growth once established.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Pogostemon Helferi Downoi Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Little star, in Thai. Pogostemon helferi — Downoi — grows low rosettes of tightly curled, ruffled leaves radiating from a central point, a shape no other foreground plant produces. Native to Thailand, and one of the few carpeting plants that prefers cooler water. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You’ll Receive

  • One 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag of Pogostemon helferi
  • Yield approx. 3-4 small plants
  • Rinse thoroughly before introducing to your aquarium

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Downoi, Thai Star Plant
  • Scientific name — Pogostemon helferi
  • Origin — Thailand
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Shipped size — Approx. 3-4 tissue-cultured plants, roughly 1-2 in
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Strong light tightens the leaf curl
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–78°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Note the ceiling — Downoi dislikes warm water
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich substrate
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Side shoots and runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Temperature is the usual reason it fails. Downoi wants 68–78°F. In a tank running at 80–82°F it goes limp, loses the curl and melts — people blame light and CO₂ when the heater is the problem.
  • The curl is a light response. Flat, uncurled leaves usually mean light isn't reaching the substrate.
  • Moderate flow suits it. Stagnant corners collect detritus in the leaf ruffles.
  • Feed at the roots — it is a heavy substrate feeder for its size.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before planting or it clouds water and feeds algae early on. Also available as loose bare-root plants.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Pogostemon Care Guide.

Notes

  • Please rinse all tissue culture plants thoroughly to remove the gel before planting. Initial melting may occur during transition, but new growth will emerge with stable conditions and care.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Balansae Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Cryptocoryne balansae grows like Vallisneria and behaves like a crypt. Long ribbon leaves with a deeply hammered, puckered surface rise a foot or more and sway with the flow — all without CO₂ or strong lighting. It is the low-tech route to a moving green background.

What You'll Receive

  • One (1) Vitro Culture® 4-inch bag of Cryptocoryne crispatula var. balansae
  • Yield: Approximately 3–4 young plantlets, ready to plant into your aquascape

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Balansae Crypt
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne crispatula var. balansae
  • Also known as — Crypt Balansae, Cryptocoryne balansae
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Background
  • Mature height — 12-20 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; this is a root feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower's Notes

  • It handles hard, alkaline water better than most crypts. Balansae comes from limestone streams, so it suits tap water that other Cryptocoryne sulk in — a genuinely useful trait if your water is hard.
  • Expect melt, then ribbon leaves. Tissue culture plantlets shed their emersed foliage as they convert. Leave the roots undisturbed; the long submersed leaves start appearing within three to six weeks.
  • The hammered texture develops with age. Young leaves come out relatively smooth. The puckered, quilted surface — the reason to buy this over Vallisneria — shows on mature growth.
  • Root tabs, not liquid dosing. A 12-20 inch leaf takes a lot of energy and crypts draw it from the substrate. Enriched soil or tabs under the crown are what produce full-length leaves.
  • Plant the crown at substrate level and then leave it. Bury the roots only. Every replant restarts the melt cycle, so choose the position before planting and let the runners spread on their own.

products.title: Ludwigia Senegalensis Guinea Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Veins you can actually see. Ludwigia senegalensis runs a network of dark red veins across brick-red to orange leaves — pattern rather than a flat block of colour, and unlike anything else in the genus. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format, which matters for a plant this sensitive to a rough start.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a Tissue Culture Plants with vitamin liquid/gel
  • Bag size: Approx. 4 inches. Yield many small plants
  • Tissue Culture Technology | 100% Free from Snail, Algae, Pathogen, and Bacteria plus Extended Shelf Life on all in Vitro Plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ludwigia Senegalensis
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia senegalensis
  • Also known as — Ludwigia sp. 'Guinea', Guinea Ludwigia
  • Origin — West Africa
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 in
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Medium to high. The vein pattern and brick-red colour both depend on it
  • CO₂ — Recommended. In practice this plant rarely performs without it
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich substrate plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim side shoots and replant

Grower's Notes

  • Stability is the requirement, not any single value. Senegalensis punishes swings in CO₂, temperature and dosing more than it punishes any particular parameter being slightly off. A settled, mature tank suits it; a new one usually does not.
  • Starting from plantlets is an advantage with this species. Cultured stock has no established growth habit to unlearn, so it adapts to your water rather than reacting to the change.
  • The veining is what you are paying for, and it needs light to show. Under weak lighting the leaves stay plain green and the pattern disappears.
  • Plant the plantlets separately with space between them. Crowded, the lower leaves shade out and the pattern is lost exactly where you would see it.
  • Frequently confused with Ludwigia glandulosa. They look similar but come from opposite sides of the Atlantic — glandulosa is North American, this is West African.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Ludwigia Care Guide.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Retrospiralis Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Tall, ribbon-like leaves that twist along their length. Cryptocoryne retrospiralis is one of the few crypts that works as a background plant — it gives a planted tank vertical movement without the trimming a stem plant demands. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You'll Receive

  • 1x Cryptocoryne Retrospiralis Vitro Culture® — grown in 4-inch bag
  • Yields approx. 3–4 healthy young plants ready for planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Retrospiralis Crypt, also known as Spiral Water Trumpet
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne retrospiralis
  • Origin — India
  • Placement — Background
  • Mature height — 10-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required, though it speeds establishment
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs under the crown.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette; also grows emersed, so it suits paludariums
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower's Notes

  • A background plant that does not need cutting. Stem plants reach the surface and then need weekly trimming. Retrospiralis grows to height and stops, which is the entire argument for using a crypt at the back of a low-maintenance tank.
  • Crypt melt is expected and is not failure. Tissue culture plantlets shed their emersed leaves as they convert to submersed growth. Leave the roots undisturbed — new leaves come from the crown within three to six weeks.
  • Plant the crown at substrate level. Bury the roots and leave the growing point exposed. A buried crown rots from the centre.
  • Feed the roots and give it depth. A tall crypt needs a deep, well-fed substrate to anchor and fuel 16 inches of leaf. Root tabs or aquasoil; two inches of substrate minimum.
  • It spreads by runner. Once settled it sends up new plants around the mother — leave space behind it and the stand thickens on its own over a year or two.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Cryptocoryne Care Guide.

Notes

Like many Cryptocoryne species, Cryptocoryne retrospiralis may undergo a temporary "crypt melt" when adapting to a new aquarium environment. This is a normal process. Once established, new growth will emerge and the plant will stabilize.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Echinodorus Rainbow
products.body_html:
Most sword plants give you one colour. Echinodorus 'Rainbow' gives you marbled leaves running white, pale green, yellow, pink and red on the same plant — a hybrid derived from Echinodorus cordifolius 'Harbich Red'. It grows slowly and feeds heavily at the roots, so what it asks for is patience and a well-fed substrate rather than difficulty.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose bare-root plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 1 individual bare-root plants
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 1 plants bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 1 plants rooted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Rainbow Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus 'Rainbow'
  • Also known as — Dwarf Rainbow Sword
  • Parentage — Derived from Echinodorus cordifolius 'Harbich Red'
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10–16 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — nutrient substrate and root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on flower stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Root tabs are not optional. This is a heavy root feeder — it takes almost everything it needs from the substrate. In inert gravel with liquid dosing alone it stalls and the colours wash out, and people mistake that for the plant being difficult.
  • Slow growth is normal. Rainbow is not a fast sword. Expect a few leaves a season, not a flush of new growth every month — which is also why it stays in proportion in a mid-sized tank.
  • Variegation can revert. Under weak light or thin feeding a marbled plant will often start pushing plain green leaves. Steady light and root feeding are what hold the colour.
  • It propagates from flower stalks, not runners. A settled plant sends up an inflorescence carrying plantlets along its length. Let each grow roots and three or four leaves before cutting it free.
  • Expect the first set of leaves to melt as it converts from emersed growth. Leave the crown planted — at substrate level, never below — and wait for the second flush, which shows the real colours.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Amazon Sword (Echinodorus) Care Guide.

Notes

  • Some leaf melt may occur as the plant transitions from emersed to submerged growth. New leaves will adapt and thrive under proper conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Anubias Petite Snow White Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Cream-white marbling on leaves under an inch across. Anubias sp. 'Petite Snow White' is one of the most heavily variegated Anubias in the hobby — and, for exactly that reason, one of the least forgiving. This is the sterile tissue-culture format.

What You'll Receive

  • One (1) Vitro Culture® 4-inch bag of Anubias sp. 'Petite Snow White'
  • Yield: Approximately 3–4 small young plants, ready to plant or attach to hardscape

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Petite Snow White Anubias
  • Scientific name — Anubias sp. 'Petite Snow White'
  • Origin — Cultivated hybrid; the genus is native to West and Central Africa
  • Placement — Midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Very slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Low to medium. Excess light burns the pale tissue and feeds algae — the single most common way this plant is lost.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Improves vigour under otherwise stable conditions.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5. Stability matters more than any particular value.
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte; attaches to wood or stone.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division, once well established

Grower's Notes

  • Cream-white tissue carries no chlorophyll, which is what makes this Advanced. The more white a leaf holds, the less energy the plant produces — so it grows very slowly, recovers badly from damage, and cannot outgrow algae on the pale areas. Anubias is famously indestructible; this cultivar is the exception that proves it.
  • It can revert. Heavily variegated Anubias sometimes starts pushing plain green leaves. Remove fully green shoots promptly — green tissue photosynthesises better and will gradually take the plant over if left.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie or glue it to wood or stone and leave it exposed; buried rhizomes rot, and this plant will not grow back from that quickly.
  • Rinse the gel off gently with aquarium or dechlorinated water — not tap — and separate the plantlets before attaching.
  • The sterile format matters more here than on a hardy plant: an algae outbreak arriving with the plant is very hard to clear from white leaves that grow this slowly.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Anubias Care Guide.

Notes

Pictures shown are for reference only. Actual plant size, shape, and variegation pattern may vary depending on growing conditions. This Vitro Culture® bag is sealed for freshness — please follow proper sterilization and acclimation procedures upon opening.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Parva
products.body_html:
Want a foreground carpet that never needs trimming? Cryptocoryne parva is the smallest true Crypt in the hobby — short narrow green rosettes that spread by runner into a neat low carpet, and grow slowly enough that you can leave them alone for months.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Cryptocoryne Parva cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in convenient planting formats:

  • Small Bare-root Portion: One healthy bare-root division with an established root system and multiple leaves, ready to plant directly into your aquarium.
  • Rooted Potted Plant: One healthy rooted plant securely grown in a nursery pot with rockwool for easy planting and faster establishment.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Parva Crypt, Crypt Parva
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne parva
  • Origin — Sri Lanka
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Mature height — 1–3 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required! One of the very few carpets that works in a low-tech tank
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Feeding — Root feeder; nutrient substrate or root tabs matter here
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Patience is the whole job. Parva is the slowest carpeting plant we sell — a full foreground takes the better part of a year. In exchange it holds its shape without trimming and lasts for years.
  • Plant individual portions with a little space between crowns and let the runners fill in. Packed tight, they shade each other before they spread.
  • Expect it to melt after planting. Crypts drop their leaves on a change of conditions, then regrow from the roots over two to four weeks. Leave it alone through that.
  • Feed at the roots. In inert gravel it survives but never builds the dense carpet you bought it for.
  • Place it once. Crypts melt again every time they are moved, and Parva is slow enough that a second melt costs months.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Cryptocoryne Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference; leaf size, count and colour vary with lighting and nutrients. Most plants are grown emersed and change appearance as they convert to submerged growth.

products.title: Rotala Green Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Rotala rotundifolia 'Green' is the plant to reach for when you want the shape of a Rotala hedge without the demands that come with the red forms. Round green leaves, fast upright growth, and no CO₂ requirement — it fills the back of a low-tech tank faster than almost anything else in the catalogue.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a Tissue Culture plants with vitamin liquid/gel
  • Bag size: Approx. 4 inches. Yield many small plants
  • Sustainable growth aquarium plants species
  • Tissue Culture Technology | 100% Free from Snail, Algae, Pathogen, and Bacteria plus Extended Shelf Life on all in Vitro Plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Rotala Green
  • Scientific name — Rotala rotundifolia 'Green'
  • Also known as — Rotala indica 'Green', Rotala sp. 'Green', Green Compact
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 8-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; also feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • Light angle decides the shape. Under medium light the stems grow straight up. Under strong light directly overhead they stay short and lean sideways, which is why aquascapers sometimes use this variety low and trimmed rather than as a background stem.
  • Rinse and portion the tissue culture before planting. Wash the gel off completely, then split the clump into groups of three or four plantlets. Planted as one mass, the centre rots before it roots.
  • The first submersed leaves look different. Emersed-grown plantlets have thicker, rounder foliage. New underwater growth is narrower and brighter — that is the plant adapting, not failing.
  • Trim above a node and it doubles. Each cut stem sends out two side shoots, so a few rounds of trimming turn six starter plantlets into a solid green thicket.
  • It grows fast enough to compete with algae. Heavy nutrient uptake makes this a useful starter plant in a newly cycled tank, where it soaks up ammonia and nitrate that would otherwise feed an algae bloom.

products.body_html:
Attaching Bucephalandra is the slow part — tying rhizomes to wood, waiting months for them to grip. This is that work already done. A mixed Buce planting grown into a natural coconut-shell pad, ready to drop straight into a tank and move around until it looks right.

Each piece is randomly picked, with random varieties and a unique shape that approx. 1x2 inches in size. It may be a bit bigger or smaller in size depending on the variety.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Buce, Bucep
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. (Grower's Choice)
  • Also known as — Tribe Schismatoglottideae, family Araceae
  • Origin — Borneo, Indonesia
  • Placement — Foreground to midground; sits on the substrate or on hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed; the pad sits on top and the rhizomes stay in open water
  • Growth habit — Amphibious epiphyte, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Do not bury the pad. Set it on the substrate or wedge it between rocks. Pushing it under gravel buries the rhizomes underneath, and buried Buce rhizomes rot.
  • It is meant to be moved. The whole point of a pad is that you can lift it, reposition it, or take it out for a water change without disturbing anything else. Use that — try it in a few spots before deciding.
  • Expect roughly an inch of growth a year. Bucephalandra is among the slowest plants sold. The pad will look much as it does now for a long time, which is exactly why it works as a permanent feature.
  • Keep the light low. A slow plant under bright light collects algae faster than it grows new leaves. Low to medium light keeps the leaves clean and holds the blues and purples better.

products.title: Dwarf Sagittaria Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Want a grass carpet without CO₂? Sagittaria subulata is the plant that gets most people there. It spreads by runners on its own, tolerates low light, and — unusually — changes height with your lighting: short and tight under bright light, taller and more ribbon-like in shade. That makes one plant do foreground or midground work depending where you put it. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You’ll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag or 2.5-inch cup containing healthy Sagittaria subulata plantlets—carefully grown, ready to rinse, acclimate, and plant.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Dwarf Sagittaria
  • Scientific name — Sagittaria subulata
  • Also known as — Dwarf Sag, Awl-leaf arrowhead
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 4–8 in, shorter under strong light
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Brighter light keeps it low and compact
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Light controls height, not growth. If your Sag is running tall and floppy, it isn't sick — it's reaching. More light brings it down. This is the single most useful thing to know about the plant.
  • It feeds at the roots. Without a nutrient substrate or root tabs, runners slow and new plantlets stay small.
  • Runners travel where they like. Trim stray runners at the substrate to keep the carpet inside its boundary.
  • Expect a pause after planting. Tissue-culture plantlets convert from emersed to submerged form over two to three weeks before they start running.
  • Plant the plantlets in small clumps an inch apart rather than one big mass — they fill the gaps themselves and root faster in small groups.

products.title: Hornwort
products.body_html:
Want a plant that fights algae for you? Hornwort grows without roots, floating or tucked into decor, and strips nutrients from the water fast enough to starve algae out. It also releases compounds that suppress algae directly — one of very few aquarium plants that does.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as loose fresh-cut plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual, loose-cut stems without root

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Hornwort, Coontail
  • Scientific name — Ceratophyllum demersum
  • Placement — Floating or background
  • Mature height — 10–20 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 64–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. It has no roots and feeds entirely from the water column
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic. Cannot be grown emersed
  • Propagation — Stem cuttings

Grower’s Notes

  • It has no roots and never will. Those pale threads are modified leaves, not roots — planting the base in substrate just rots it. Let it float, or wedge a stem between rocks or wood to anchor it.
  • Expect needle drop on arrival and after any big change. Hornwort sheds when conditions shift and regrows within a week or two. The mess is temporary; keep the firm green stems.
  • It tolerates cold. Comfortable from 64°F, which makes it one of the few plants that works in an unheated tank, a goldfish tank or a pond.
  • Trim and replant tops, discard bare stems. Like most fast stems, the lower section goes bare and does not refoliate.
  • It grows fast enough to shade everything below. Thin it every week or two rather than letting the mat close over.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Hornwort Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference. Hornwort is a delicate, rootless plant and may shed some needles during shipping or after introduction — this is normal and it will regrow quickly under stable conditions.
  • Hornwort is considered invasive in certain regions and may be restricted or prohibited. Check your local and state regulations before purchasing, and never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

featured_image.alt: Ceratophyllum demersum, commonly known as Hornwort, is a popular and versatile aquatic plant that enhances the beauty and health of any aquarium. Known for its hardy nature and rapid growth, Hornwort is an excellent choice for both beginner and experienced aquarists.

products.title: Anubias Petite White Platinum Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Almost no green at all. Anubias barteri var. nana 'Petite White Platinum' carries pale white, cream and platinum foliage with very little chlorophyll — an effectively albino nano Anubias. Against dark driftwood or black lava rock it reads as a light source. It is also, for the same reason, one of the slowest and most demanding plants we sell.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Anubias Petite White Platinum Vitro Culture® cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®.

Sold in a sealed 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag.

Each bag typically yields approximately 3 small plant clumps after rinsing and separating from the nutrient gel.

Plant size, leaf count, and clump size may vary slightly due to natural growth differences.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Petite White Platinum Anubias
  • Scientific name — Anubias barteri var. nana 'Petite White Platinum'
  • Also known as — Anubias White Nano Petite
  • Placement — Midground, attached to driftwood, stone or lava rock
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Growth rate — Very slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced. Almost no chlorophyll means almost no energy production
  • Light — Low to medium, steady. Intense light burns pale tissue
  • CO₂ — Not required, but stable conditions are
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5. Consistency matters more than any specific value
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape

  • Propagation — Rhizome division once mature

  • This is the hardest Anubias we sell. White Platinum has less green pigment than Pinto or Panda Marble, so it produces less energy than either — growth is measured in a leaf or two per season, and there is effectively no margin for a bad month. Buy it as a collector plant, not a workhorse.

  • Never bury the rhizome. Glue or tie it to hardscape, tucking the roots around rather than under.

products.title: Rotala Rotundifolia
products.body_html:
The Rotala to start with. Rotala rotundifolia grows small round leaves in opposite pairs on fast, upright stems, and shifts from bright green to a pink or reddish tone under strong light. It's the most forgiving plant in a genus with a reputation for being demanding — and it grows fast enough to fill a background in weeks.

What You’ll Receive

products.title: Pogostemon Helferi
products.body_html:
Want a foreground plant that looks like nothing else? Pogostemon helferi grows tightly curled, deeply serrated leaves in a low rosette — the Thai name dao noi means "little star", which is exactly what a healthy plant looks like from above.

What You’ll Receive

  • Scientific name — Pogostemon helferi

  • Mature height — 2–4 in

  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder

Grower’s Notes

  • It wants cooler water than most. Downoi tops out around 78°F, noticeably lower than the 82°F most of our plants tolerate. In a warm tank it stretches, loses the tight rosette form and struggles — this is the requirement most often missed.
  • Plant rosettes an inch or two apart and let them spread. Each plant throws side shoots from the base rather than growing upward.
  • Expect melt on arrival. It reacts to a change of conditions by dropping leaves, then rebuilds from the centre. Leave it alone for two to three weeks.
  • Feed at the roots. In inert gravel the leaves come in smaller and flatter, losing the curl that makes it worth buying.
  • Also available as sterile Downoi Vitro Culture, or the rare White Albino form.

products.body_html:

products.body_html:

Myriophyllum mattogrossense 'Golden' carries the same fine feathered whorls as the standard species, but under strong light the foliage runs very pale yellow to nearly white, sometimes with reddish tips. It is a striking plant and a demanding one — the colour comes from low pigment, which makes it slow to recover and quick to show algae.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Myriophyllum mattogrossense 'Golden' Vitro Culture® grown in sterile laboratory conditions and sealed in 4-inch tissue culture bags.

Choose your preferred pack size:

  • Pack 5 — 5 × 4-inch Vitro Culture® bags, each yielding many small plantlets

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Golden Mattogrossense Milfoil
  • Scientific name — Myriophyllum mattogrossense 'Golden'
  • Also known as — Golden Watermilfoil, White Milfoil
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Brazil

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate

  • CO₂ — Recommended. Pale foliage photosynthesises less, so carbon matters more here than on the green form
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0

Grower’s Notes

  • Put it in a mature tank, not a new one. This is the single thing that decides whether it works. Pale leaves carry little chlorophyll, so the plant cannot outgrow algae — and algae settling on golden foliage destroys the colour you bought it for. A stable, established tank with good algae control is close to a requirement.

  • Plant stems individually an inch apart. Fine whorls shade each other badly when a bunch goes in as one lump.
  • Trim and replant the tops. It branches readily from below the cut, and repeated topping builds a dense group.
  • Pair it against dark green or red planting — the contrast is most of the effect. The standard green Mattogrossense is far more forgiving if you want the texture without the difficulty.

products.title: Glossostigma Elatinoides Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Glossostigma elatinoides is the carpet that defined the Iwagumi look — leaves the size of a grain of rice, spreading flat across the substrate in a dense green mat. It is also the carpet that punishes shortcuts. Given the light and CO₂ it asks for, nothing covers ground faster.

What You'll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing healthy Glossostigma elatinoides plantlets—ready to rinse, acclimate, and plant in your aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Glosso
  • Scientific name — Glossostigma elatinoides
  • Also known as — Glosso, mud mat
  • Origin — New Zealand and southeastern Australia
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Mature height — 0.5-1 inch
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High
  • CO₂ — Required
  • Water — 68-78°F, pH 6.0-7.0
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil, or inert sand with root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious creeper, root feeder
  • Propagation — Runners; trim and replant to even out coverage

Grower's Notes

  • Light intensity decides whether it carpets or climbs. Under high light Glosso lies flat and runs sideways. Under weak light it stretches upward on bare stems reaching for the surface, and the carpet never closes. This single variable causes most Glosso failures.
  • Plant in small portions, not clumps. Separate the tissue culture mat into pinches of two or three plantlets and set them roughly an inch apart. Dense clumps shade their own bases and rot from underneath.
  • Trim the carpet before it layers. Once coverage closes, Glosso grows over itself. The buried lower layer dies, loses grip, and the mat lifts off the substrate in sheets. Cut it back to a low, thin layer every few weeks.
  • Tissue culture melt is expected. Emersed-grown plantlets shed their first set of leaves as they convert to submersed growth. Keep CO₂ and light steady rather than adjusting them, and new flat growth follows within two weeks.
  • It is a heavy root feeder. On inert sand or gravel, Glosso pales and thins no matter how good the lighting is. Root tabs beneath the planting area are not optional.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete guide to preparing tissue culture plants.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference only. Plant size, density, and color may vary depending on lighting and aquarium conditions. Glossostigma may melt during transition from tissue culture but will regrow under stable care.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Ludwigia Pantanal Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
One of the hardest reds worth growing. Ludwigia inclinata var. verticillata 'Pantanal' carries narrow needle-like leaves in whorls, colouring from pink through to fiery red — a texture and colour combination almost nothing else in the hobby offers. It also demands high light, CO₂ and soft water to show it. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You'll Receive

  • 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag of Ludwigia Pantanal
  • Each bag contains multiple healthy plantlets, ready for immediate planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ludwigia Pantanal
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia sp. 'Pantanal'
  • Also known as — Ludwigia inclinata var. verticillata 'Pantanal'
  • Origin — Pantanal wetlands, South America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 6–14 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. High light is what produces the red
  • CO₂ — Recommended, in practice near-essential for colour
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Soft, low-carbonate water with good flow
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich substrate
  • Growth habit — Amphibious, but colours and forms best submerged

Grower's Notes

  • Pantanal punishes instability. It reacts to swings in CO₂, light period or fertilisation faster than almost any other stem plant — usually by dropping its lower leaves. Have the tank running steadily before you add it.
  • Soft water is not optional. Pantanal wants low carbonate hardness. In hard alkaline tap water it stunts at the tips whatever else you do — test KH rather than chasing a pH number.
  • Good flow matters as much as light. Stagnant water shows up as stunted tips.
  • Trim the tops and replant them — cuttings colour faster than the stumps regrow. Tissue culture removes the pest risk but not the demands, so expect a short adaptation period and green early growth.
  • If this is a step too far, Ludwigia Super Red Mini gives deep red on a far more forgiving plant.

Care

  • Difficulty: Intermediate
  • Light: Medium to high. It grows green under medium light and shifts toward orange and red as intensity rises.
  • CO₂: Recommended. Injection tightens the node spacing and deepens the color; without it the stems grow leggier and stay green.
  • Water: pH 6.0-7.5, 72-82°F (22-28°C)
  • Substrate: Required — a nutrient-rich substrate or root tabs, with water column dosing alongside
  • Growth habit: Upright stems with narrow, lance-shaped leaves and compact nodes
  • Propagation: Cuttings — trim healthy stems and replant the tops

Grower's Notes

  • Trim it hard and often. Fast growth is only useful if you use it. Cutting the group back by a third every couple of weeks forces side shoots and builds the dense bush this plant is capable of.
  • Replant the tops and discard the old bases. Cuttings root within days and outgrow the stumps they came from.
  • Space stems roughly an inch apart when planting. Bundled stems shade each other and rot at the center.
  • Still uncommon outside specialist collections. 'Wayanad' has never been assigned a species epithet and circulates under its collection locality.
  • Expect the emersed-grown tissue culture foliage to melt back before submerged leaves appear. New growth is the honest signal.

Notes

  • Images are for reference. Color intensity and plant form will vary depending on lighting, nutrients, and tank conditions. Initial melting may occur during the transition from tissue culture, followed by healthy regrowth under optimal care.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Dwarf Baby Tears
products.body_html:
The finest carpet in the hobby, and the least forgiving. Dwarf Baby Tears — HC Cuba — has leaves a few millimetres across, so a healthy carpet reads at a scale nothing else matches. It also wants high light, CO₂, and water below 78°F. Get those right and it carpets fast; get them wrong and it lifts off the substrate in sheets.

What You’ll Receive

Select the format that best fits your aquascape:

  • Fresh-cut Plants
    Small loose clusters of HC (approx. 1"x1"), ideal for immediate planting and the most efficient way to establish a healthy HC carpet.
  • Rooted Bunched Plants
    Healthy stems tied with weight for quick anchoring and faster establishment.
  • Rooted Potted Plants
    Fully rooted plants grown in rockwool — the easiest to transition and quickest to carpet.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Dwarf Baby Tears, HC Cuba
  • Scientific name — Micranthemum callitrichoides 'Cuba'
  • Also known as — Hemianthus callitrichoides 'Cuba' (the older name, still in wide use), HC Cuba, HC
  • Origin — Cuba
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Shipped size — Small clusters approx. 1"x1", or rooted portions
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Suits — 5 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast, once established

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High. Light must reach the substrate, not just the surface
  • CO₂ — Required
  • Water — 68–78°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Note the ceiling — HC struggles in warm tanks
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich soil
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Runners and stolons

Grower’s Notes

  • Temperature is the overlooked failure. People blame light and CO₂ when a carpet melts, but HC does poorly above about 78°F. In a tank running at 80–82°F for discus or similar, it will not hold — use Monte Carlo instead.
  • Two names, one plant. Most of the hobby knows it as Hemianthus callitrichoides; the accepted name is now Micranthemum callitrichoides. You will see both on shop shelves and in forums.
  • Plant small — three or four leaves per portion, half an inch apart. Large clumps rot in the middle and float off.
  • A carpet that lifts is a rooting problem, not a nutrient problem. Press portions firmly into fine substrate and keep flow off them until they anchor.
  • If this sounds like more than you want, Micranthemum Monte Carlo carpets in similar style with far less demand.

Want to go deeper? Read our carpet plant comparison: Dwarf Baby Tears vs Monte Carlo vs Dwarf Hairgrass.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference only. Actual plant size, shape, and density may vary based on growth stage and tank conditions. Some initial melting may occur during transition.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Dwarf Sagittaria Subulata
products.body_html:
Want a carpet you can grow without CO₂? Dwarf Sagittaria is a grass-like rosette that spreads by runner into a dense colony, with its height set by your lighting rather than by the plant. Bright light keeps it low enough for a foreground; in dimmer tanks it stretches upward and reads as midground.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as Bare-root Plants, Bunched Plants, or Potted Plants:

  • Bare-root plants | Approx. 6 loose bare-root plants
  • Bunched plants | Approx. 6 rooted plants bundled with foam and lead weight
  • Potted plants | Approx. 6 rooted plants in a net pot with rock wool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Dwarf Sagittaria, Dwarf Sag
  • Scientific name — Sagittaria subulata
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 4–8 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Grows submerged or emersed
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • It feeds almost entirely through its roots. In inert gravel or sand it stalls without root tabs — the most common reason it disappoints.
  • Want it short? Raise the light. Want height? Lower it. Trimming the blades doesn't control height and leaves cut ends that brown off.
  • Separate bundles into individual rosettes before planting. Bunches planted intact rot in the middle.
  • Plant each crown at the substrate line — buried crowns rot.
  • Because it is amphibious it also works in pond margins, paludariums and dry start setups. Emersed growth looks different — shorter and stiffer — and converts when submerged.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Dwarf Sagittaria Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference; height, blade width and colour vary considerably with lighting and nutrients.
  • Some aquatic plants are restricted in certain U.S. states — check before ordering, and never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.
