products.title: Cryptocoryne Pink Flamingo Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Want genuine pink rather than red? Cryptocoryne wendtii 'Pink Flamingo' is one of the few aquarium plants that delivers it — wavy, textured leaves in light pink to rose on a compact rosette. It is also one of the most demanding Crypts in the hobby, and worth understanding before you buy.

What You’ll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing healthy Cryptocoryne 'Pink Flamingo' plantlets — ready to rinse, acclimate, and plant in your aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pink Flamingo Crypt
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne wendtii 'Pink Flamingo'
  • Also known as — Crypt Flamingo, Cryptocoryne Pink Panther
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Sri Lanka
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 3–5 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Medium to high. Strong light intensifies the pink
  • CO₂ — Recommended. It holds colour and compact form far better with it
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Substrate runners, slowly

Grower’s Notes

  • The pink is why it is difficult. Pink leaves carry far less chlorophyll than green ones, so this plant photosynthesises less efficiently than any standard wendtii and has much less margin for poor light, unstable conditions or neglect. Treat it as an advanced plant regardless of how easy ordinary Crypt Wendtii is.
  • Expect a heavy melt. All Crypts shed leaves on a change of conditions, and Pink Flamingo does it harder than most. Leave it alone for three to four weeks and let it rebuild from the roots — pulling it up is what turns a recoverable melt into a loss.
  • Feed at the roots and don't move it. Crypts melt again every time they are relocated, and this one is slow enough that a second melt costs months.
  • New growth often returns greener before the pink comes back. Judge the colour once it has settled, not on the first leaves.

Three ways to buy this plant. This listing is the 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag — several sterile plantlets, the best value per plant. There is also an established bare-root or potted plant if you want size now, and a small Vitro Culture® cup with one small rooted plant — the cheapest way in, and the slowest.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Cryptocoryne Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are sample representations. Actual colouration may vary depending on lighting, CO₂, and nutrient availability. Melting may occur during the transition to submerged growth, but healthy regrowth is expected under stable care.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Ludwigia Tornado Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Ludwigia Tornado is the stem plant that looks like it is caught mid-spin. Each narrow leaf twists into a corkscrew as it grows, so a planted group reads as motion rather than a flat wall of foliage. Colour runs olive-green to rust and red depending on how hard the tank is driven.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Ludwigia Tornado Vitro Culture® cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in multiple value packs:

  • 1 Bag: One 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag filled with many small plantlets
  • 5 Bags: Five 4-inch Vitro Culture® bags (excellent for larger aquascapes or propagation)
  • 10 Bags: Ten 4-inch Vitro Culture® bags (ideal for larger tank coverage)

Each 4-inch bag contains multiple young plants, which can be separated and grown into numerous individual stems—offering exceptional value and flexibility for aquascaping.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Tornado Ludwigia
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia inclinata var. verticillata 'Curly'
  • Also known as — Ludwigia Twister, Ludwigia Curly
  • Origin — Central and South America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 6-14 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs, plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • The curl is a light response, not a fixed trait. Under medium light the leaves loosen and flatten out. Strong light directly overhead is what tightens them into the spiral this variety is sold for.
  • Expect straight leaves out of the bag. Tissue culture plantlets are grown emersed and arrive without the twist. The curled form appears on the new submersed growth over the following few weeks.
  • Iron drives the red. Without a comprehensive micronutrient dose the plant grows well but stays green. Regular iron dosing under strong light is what pushes the colour toward rust and wine red.
  • Separate the culture into small clusters. Rinse the gel away and plant two or three plantlets per spot, spaced about an inch apart. Planting the whole mat as one lump kills the centre.
  • Trim the tops, replant them, discard the base. Like most Ludwigia, older lower stems go leggy. Cutting the top few inches and replanting them keeps the group dense and evenly coloured.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Ludwigia Care Guide.

Notes

  • Appearance may vary depending on growing conditions. Plants may arrive in emersed form and will transition to submerged growth once planted in your aquarium. Some initial leaf melt may occur during acclimation.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Anubias Golden Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Bright yellow-green leaves in a genus that is otherwise uniformly dark. Anubias Golden holds a golden-lime tone that reads as a highlight against wood, stone and the deep green of everything else in the tank — with the same undemanding rhizome as any other Anubias. This is the sterile tissue-culture format.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a Tissue Culture Plants with vitamin liquid/gel
  • Bag size: Approx. 4 inches (yield 2-3 clump plants)
  • Sustainable growth aquatic plants species
  • Great value! Nice specimen!
  • Tissue Culture Technology | 100% Free from Snail, Algae, Pathogen, and Bacteria plus Extended Shelf Life on all in Vitro Plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Golden Anubias
  • Scientific name — Anubias barteri var. 'Golden'
  • Also known as — Anubias Golden Nana
  • Origin — Cultivated variety; the genus is native to West and Central Africa
  • Placement — Midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 4-6 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Shade suits it; strong light means algae on slow-turning leaves.
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte; attaches to wood or stone.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • The gold is new growth, not variegation. Each leaf emerges pale golden-lime and darkens toward green as it matures, so the colour sits at the growing tip rather than being fixed in the leaf. That also means it is normally pigmented — no harder to grow than any other Anubias.
  • Place it against something dark. The pale new growth is what you are paying for, and it disappears against light sand or pale stone. Dark wood or black lava rock is where it earns its price.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots can go into substrate; the rhizome cannot. Buried, it rots — the most common way an Anubias is lost.
  • Rinse the gel off completely and separate the clumps before attaching. Leftover nutrient agar clouds water and feeds algae.
  • Keep it shaded. Growth is slow enough that algae settles on a leaf faster than the plant replaces it.

Prefer a rooted plant? See Anubias Golden Nana.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Anubias Care Guide.

Notes

Disclaimer: Pictures are not the actual plants you will receive, but a sample representation. Unless specific, we don't guarantee aquatic plants will be free of pests, pesticides, grow emerged, or submerge.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Bucephalandra Deep Purple Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Deep Purple carries small, slightly wavy oval leaves running dark green through deep violet. It is one of the more reliably purple varieties — the tone holds on emersed and submersed growth alike, where many Buce lose their colour on conversion. This is the tissue-culture format.

What You'll Receive

  • One sealed 4-inch Vitro Culture® tissue culture bag
  • Approximately 4 small plantlets grown in sterile nutrient gel
  • 100% free from snails, algae, pesticides and pathogens
  • Rinse the gel away and separate the plantlets before planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Deep Purple Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Deep Purple'
  • Also known as — Buce, Bucep
  • Origin — Borneo (genus range)
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Brighter light intensifies the purple but also brings algae the plant is too slow to outgrow — medium is the practical ceiling.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Deepens colour and speeds growth if you already run it.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed. Epiphyte; attaches to wood or rock.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rhizome creeper; grows submersed or emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • The purple survives the switch to submersed growth. Many coloured Buce arrive vivid and fade to green in the tank. Deep Purple holds its tone in both forms, which is the practical reason to pick it over a variety that only colours up emersed.
  • Rinse the gel off completely and separate the four plantlets before attaching. Leftover nutrient agar clouds water and feeds algae.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie or glue it to wood or rock and leave it exposed; buried rhizomes rot.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.
  • Moderate flow suits it, mirroring the river conditions the genus comes from and keeping debris off slow-turning leaves.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Bucephalandra Care Guide.

Notes

Remove plants from the tissue culture gel and rinse gently before placing them in your aquarium. Due to the delicate nature of Vitro Culture plants, some melt may occur during transition but will regrow under stable conditions.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Microsorum Pteropus Windelov Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Leaf tips that branch and re-branch into fine crests instead of ending in a point. Leptochilus pteropus 'Windelov' — the Lace Java Fern — is the cultivar that gives a low-tech tank fine detail without needing CO₂ or bright light. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You'll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing multiple healthy plantlets:

  • Approximately 6+ leaves total
  • May arrive as individual leaves or small plantlets, not fully connected
  • Each plantlet includes developing roots for easy attachment and growth

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Lace Java Fern
  • Scientific name — Leptochilus pteropus 'Windelov' (syn. Microsorum pteropus)
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to driftwood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 4-8 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte — attach the rhizome to hardscape and never bury it.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; grows emersed as well as submersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division, plus plantlets from mature leaves

Grower's Notes

  • Rinse the gel off, and expect loose pieces. Tissue-culture Windelov often separates into individual leaves rather than a single clump. That is normal — each piece with a scrap of rhizome and a root will grow. Rinse until the roots feel clean, then attach the pieces close together.
  • Expect some melt. Leaves may die back as the plant converts from lab conditions to submerged growth. As long as the rhizome stays firm and green, new growth follows.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots may go into substrate; the green horizontal stem must stay in open water or it rots — the single most common way a Java Fern is killed.
  • Keep the light modest. Java Fern grows too slowly to outgrow algae, and algae caught in a finely branched leaf tip is close to impossible to clean out. Shade is the defence.
  • Sterile media is the point. No snails, no algae spores, no pesticide residue — which is what makes this format the right choice for a shrimp tank.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Java Fern Care Guide.

Notes

  • Tissue culture plants are grown in sterile gel and may require rinsing before planting.
  • Leaves may melt slightly during transition as the plant adapts to submerged conditions—this is normal.
  • Proper acclimation will ensure healthy new growth.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Aponogeton Boivinianus
products.body_html:
Aponogeton Boivinianus is a stunning bulb aquarium plant prized for its large, heavily textured leaves and bold presence in freshwater aquariums. Native to Madagascar, this species produces long, crinkled, deep-green leaves that create instant visual impact as a centerpiece or background plant in larger aquascapes.

Care at a glance

  • Light: Medium to high
  • CO₂: Not required (recommended for stronger growth)
  • Temperature: 72–82°F (22–28°C)
  • Water Parameters: Soft to moderately hard
  • Placement: Midground/Background

What You'll Receive

  • Healthy Aponogeton Boivinianus cultivated by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in two variants:
  • Bulb Only: A firm, healthy bulb ready to sprout
  • Sprouted Bulb with Leaf: A healthy bulb with approximately 3–4 new sprouting leaves, already showing active growth

Disclaimer: Growth rate, leaf size, and overall appearance may vary depending on aquarium conditions. Minor leaf melt can occur during acclimation. Please never release aquatic plants into local waterways.

products.title: Bucephalandra Red Catherine
products.body_html:
Red Catherine is one of the darker Bucephalandra varieties we grow — narrow, elongated leaves that hold a red-to-bronze tone rather than the blue-green of the common Buce types. It stays small, grows slowly, and needs no substrate at all.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose Bare-Root or Potted plants:

  • 1 Bare-Root: Approximately 6+ leaves
  • 5 Bare-Root: Approximately 30+ leaves total
  • 10 Bare-Root: Approximately 60+ leaves total
  • 1 Potted: Approximately 10+ leaves
  • 5 Potted: Approximately 50+ leaves total
  • 10 Potted: Approximately 100+ leaves total

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Red Catherine Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Red Catherine'
  • Also known as — Buce Red Catherine
  • Origin — Borneo (genus range)
  • Placement — Midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 3-5 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Stronger light deepens the red and bronze tones; it will still grow under low light, just greener.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Improves growth rate and color if you already run it.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed. Epiphyte; feeds from the water column.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rhizome creeper; grows submersed or emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie or glue the horizontal rhizome to wood or rock and leave it exposed. Buried rhizomes rot.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.
  • Some leaf melt after shipping is normal. The rhizome survives it and pushes new submersed leaves within a few weeks — don't throw the plant away.
  • Red Catherine's color sits in the leaf itself rather than in a surface sheen, so it reads red across a wider range of viewing angles than the iridescent varieties.
  • Growth is slow enough that it rarely needs trimming. Plan the placement once and leave it.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Bucephalandra Care Guide.

Notes

Like most Bucephalandra, minor leaf melt may occur after introduction as the plant adjusts to new water parameters. This is normal and temporary — new submersed leaves regrow from the rhizome once the plant stabilizes.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Anubias Nana Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
The plant that survives almost anything, in a form that introduces nothing. Anubias barteri var. nana grows in low light without CO₂, attaches to wood and stone, and its thick leathery leaves resist fish that shred softer plants. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format — no snails, no algae, no pesticide residue to worry about in a shrimp tank.

What You’ll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing approximately 3 healthy Anubias Nana plantlets—ready to rinse, acclimate, and plant in your aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Nana Anubias
  • Scientific name — Anubias barteri var. nana
  • Placement — Midground, attached to wood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 4–6 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Strong light means algae on slow-turning leaves
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower’s Notes

  • Tissue culture plantlets start small. These are young plants, not mature rhizomes — cheaper per plant and completely clean, but give them a few months before they look like the photos. If you want size now, buy the bare-root or potted Anubias Nana.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Glue or tie it to wood or stone; roots can enter substrate, the rhizome cannot.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before attaching, or it feeds algae in the first weeks.
  • Slow growth means very little maintenance, but damaged leaves stay damaged. Trim old leaves at the rhizome.
  • Tough enough for cichlid and large-fish tanks where softer planting gets destroyed.

products.title: Aponogeton Madagascariensis (Madagascar Lace)
products.body_html:
Leaves with the tissue missing. Aponogeton madagascariensis grows foliage that is pure lattice — a skeleton of veins with open holes where leaf blade would normally be. No other aquarium plant looks remotely like it. It is also genuinely demanding: cool, clean, moving water, and patience.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as Bare-root Plants, Sprouts Bulb With Leaf, or Bulb Without Leaf:
  • Bare-root Plants: A healthy loose specimen without bulb
  • Sprouted Bulb with Leaf: A healthy bulb with at least two lace leaf already growing
  • Bulb Only (No Leaf): A firm, viable bulb without current foliage (ideal for patient aquarists)

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Madagascar Lace Plant
  • Scientific name — Aponogeton madagascariensis
  • Origin — Slow rivers and lakes of Madagascar
  • Plant type — Bulb / tuber
  • Placement — Background or centrepiece
  • Mature height — 10–16 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Medium to high, but indirect. Harsh light burns the open leaf structure
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68–75°F · pH 6.0–7.0. The temperature ceiling is the strictest of any plant we sell
  • Flow — Gentle to moderate, well oxygenated. Stagnant water rots the bulb
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — True aquatic. Does not grow emersed
  • Propagation — Bulb offsets

Grower’s Notes

  • Temperature is what kills it. Above about 75°F the lace plant declines regardless of everything else. In a standard tropical community tank at 78–82°F it will not survive long — this plant needs a cool, well-oxygenated tank of its own terms.
  • Clean water matters more than fertiliser. The open leaf structure traps detritus and grows algae easily; steady flow and regular water changes keep it clear.
  • Expect a dormancy. Lace plants often drop all their leaves and rest for weeks or months. Leave the bulb in place — it usually restarts.
  • Press the bulb only partly into the substrate; fully buried bulbs rot.
  • Buy the sprouted bulb if you want certainty. A bare bulb is cheaper but asks for patience with no guarantee.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Aponogeton Care Guide.

Notes

  • This is a sensitive and specialty plant not suited for beginners. Water quality, cool temperature, and stable parameters are key to long-term success. Bulbs may take time to adjust after shipping — please plant with care and patience.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Hydrocotyle Tripartita
products.body_html:
Want a carpet with recognisable leaves? Hydrocotyle tripartita creeps across the substrate on fine stems carrying bright green clover-shaped leaves — far more distinct at a glance than the grass and moss textures most carpets offer. It also climbs, which is where it gets interesting.

What You’ll Receive

Choose the format that suits your aquascaping needs:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Loose, freshly cut portion without root, ready to be planted or attached
  • Bunched Plants: Fresh-cut stems without root bundled with foam and plant weight for easy anchoring
  • Potted Plants: Fresh-cut stems without root potted in rockwool and net pot for stable placement and easy handling

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Hydrocotyle Japan
  • Scientific name — Hydrocotyle tripartita
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Strong light keeps it flat; weak light makes it climb
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Creeping runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Light decides whether it carpets or climbs. Under strong light reaching the substrate it stays flat and spreads sideways. Under weaker light it grows upward, scrambling over rock and wood — which some aquascapers do on purpose for a vine effect.
  • Trim it often. It grows fast and will smother slower neighbours within weeks if left — this is a plant that needs managing, not a set-and-forget carpet.
  • Replant the trimmings. Every cut piece roots readily, so one portion covers a foreground quickly at no extra cost.
  • It attaches loosely to hardscape as it creeps, so you can wrap it around stone and let it hold on by itself.

products.title: Amazon Sword (Small Size)
products.body_html:
The same Amazon Sword, bought small. Echinodorus bleheri ships here at 4-6 inches — a cheaper way into a plant that will still reach a foot and a half, and a size that suits a newly planted tank where a full specimen would look out of scale from day one.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Amazon Sword (Small Size) (Echinodorus bleheri) cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®.

Available in multiple growth forms:

  • Bare-root Plant — one healthy bare-root plant approximately 4–6 inches tall
  • Rooted Bunched — one rooted bunch containing approximately 1–2 healthy plants, secured with aquarium-safe foam and a plant weight
  • Rooted Potted — one healthy rooted plant grown in a nursery pot for easy planting

Simply plant the roots into a nutrient-rich substrate while keeping the crown (where the leaves emerge) above the substrate surface.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Amazon Sword, also known as Broad Leaf Amazon Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus bleheri
  • Also known as — Echinodorus grisebachii 'Bleherae'
  • Origin — South America
  • Placement — Midground while young, background or centrepiece once grown
  • Shipped size — 4-6 inches
  • Mature height — 12-20 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner, provided you feed the roots
  • Light — Medium. It reaches full size without high-output lighting.
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required. Steady growth either way.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — root tabs are not optional in inert gravel.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on aerial floral stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Small is the shipping size, not the plant. This will not stay 4-6 inches. Under normal aquarium conditions it becomes the same 12-20 inch rosette as the full-size listing — so plant it where a large plant can live, not where a small one fits.
  • Feed it at the roots from the start. A young sword in inert gravel yellows, thins and develops holes in the older leaves. Root tabs or aquasoil under the crown are what turn a small plant into a large one.
  • Give it three inches of substrate depth. Set the crown at the surface, never below. The root mass gets substantial and a shallow bed stunts it permanently.
  • It propagates by floral stalk, not runner. Once settled it throws a tall stalk carrying plantlets. Leave each attached until it has four or five leaves and its own roots, then cut it free and plant it.
  • Expect a transition. Grown emersed, so some arriving leaves may die back as it converts to submerged growth. New leaves follow from the crown.

Other ways to buy this plant. Standard grade is the Amazon Sword; there is also a mother plant at 16-24 inches and a bulk pack.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Amazon Sword Care Guide.

Notes

Pictures are representative samples only. Live aquatic plants are natural products and may vary in size, color, and fullness depending on season and growing conditions. Plants are shipped approximately 4–6 inches tall and will continue to grow significantly larger under proper aquarium conditions. Amazon Sword is commonly grown emersed and may experience a normal transition period as it adapts to submerged aquarium conditions.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Bucephalandra Petite Blue Chili Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Petite Blue Chili is a nano Bucephalandra with an unusually wide colour range — blue, violet, green and metallic tones that develop once the plant converts to submersed growth and shift with the tank it is in. At one to three inches it works as detail rather than mass.

What You'll Receive

  • One sealed 4-inch Vitro Culture® tissue culture bag
  • Approximately 4 small plantlets grown in sterile nutrient gel
  • 100% free from snails, algae, pesticides and pathogens
  • Rinse the gel away and separate the plantlets before planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Petite Blue Chili Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Petite Blue Chili'
  • Also known as — Buce Blue Chili
  • Origin — Borneo (genus range)
  • Placement — Foreground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 1-3 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Leaves this small have no margin for algae, so keep it down.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Deepens colour and speeds growth if you already run it.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed. Epiphyte; attaches to rock or driftwood.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rhizome creeper; grows submersed or emersed. Can flower year-round.
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Gentle flow suits it, mirroring the river it comes from. Bucephalandra are rheophytes — they grow on rock in moving water. Current keeps debris off the leaves, but too much lifts a small rhizome off its mount before the roots grip.
  • Rinse the gel off completely and separate the four plantlets before attaching. Leftover nutrient agar clouds water and feeds algae.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie or glue it to wood or rock and leave it exposed; buried rhizomes rot.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.
  • Colour is a property of your tank as much as the plant. Blue and violet develop over weeks under the right spectrum; under warm white the same plant reads plain green.

products.title: Micro Sword Narrow Leaf
products.body_html:
Micro Sword Narrow Leaf is the finest-bladed of the Lilaeopsis carpets. Where the standard micro sword reads as short grass, this one reads as fine turf — thin, upright blades that spread by runner into a low meadow with a much more delicate scale.

What You'll Receive

Choose the format that best suits your planting style:

  • Bare-root Plants — Small loose clusters, ideal for direct planting and precise spacing across the foreground.
  • Rooted Bunched Plants — Healthy rooted stems tied with weight for fast anchoring and easy placement.
  • Rooted Potted Plants — Fully rooted plants grown in rockwool, the easiest to plant and fastest to establish.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Narrow Leaf Micro Sword
  • Scientific name — Lilaeopsis mauritiana
  • Also known as — Micro Sword Narrow Leaf, Mauritius Micro Sword
  • Origin — Mauritius
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Mature height — 1-3 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; this is a root feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower's Notes

  • Split it into small plugs and space them out. Separate the portion into clusters of a few blades with roots attached and plant them an inch apart. Lilaeopsis fills the gaps by runner far faster than one clump grows outward.
  • It is slow to start and then steady. Expect very little visible progress for the first three or four weeks while the roots establish, then runners in every direction. Do not disturb it during the quiet phase.
  • Feed the roots. This carpet takes almost everything from the substrate. On inert sand without root tabs it survives but barely spreads; over aquasoil it closes properly.
  • Light reaches the base or the base dies. Once the carpet thickens, trim it back. Shaded lower blades brown off, lose grip and the mat lifts in patches.
  • Finer than standard micro sword. If you have used Lilaeopsis brasiliensis and found it coarse for a nano tank, this is the version to use — same habit, noticeably thinner blades.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference only. Actual plant size and density may vary. Some initial transition melting may occur as the plant adapts to submerged growth.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Fissidens Nobilis
products.body_html:
Feathers, not fuzz. Fissidens nobilis grows flat, distinctly feather-shaped fronds in a single plane — and at a noticeably larger scale than Phoenix Moss, so the individual fronds are visible rather than merging into a mass. The most structured-looking moss we carry.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a small loose portion
  • Approx. 2" x 2" in size
  • Perfect to attached to driftwood, rock, or stone

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Noble Fissidens
  • Scientific name — Fissidens nobilis
  • Placement — Foreground, attached to driftwood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required, though it thickens growth
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Fragmentation — divide and re-attach

Grower’s Notes

  • Frond size is what you're paying for. Most mosses read as texture from a distance. Nobilis is large enough that the feather shape stays legible — use it where it will be seen up close, not as background filler.
  • Tie it thinly and flat. The fronds grow in one plane, so pressing it flat against wood or stone gives the best result; a thick pad hides the structure and rots underneath.
  • Slow growth means it holds its shape for months without trimming — but also that algae, once in it, is very hard to clear.
  • Keep light moderate and flow steady; stagnant corners let detritus settle between the fronds.
  • Divide with scissors and re-attach the pieces — each fragment establishes independently.

products.title: Anubias Panda Marble
products.body_html:
No two are the same. Anubias barteri 'Panda Marble' — introduced by Aquarium Plants Factory® in 2024 — carries unpredictable marbling of white, cream and green across thick coin-shaped leaves. The pattern varies leaf to leaf and plant to plant, which is the appeal and also the reason this is an advanced plant rather than a typical easy Anubias.

What You’ll Receive

Enhance your aquarium with our fresh, high-quality plants, available in convenient formats:

  • Loose Bare-Root Plants: Includes approximately 6 or more leaves of bare-root plants for flexible placement.
  • Rooted Potted Plants: Includes approximately 6 or more leaves, rooted in a net pot with rock wool for easy installation.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Panda Marble Anubias
  • Scientific name — Anubias barteri 'Panda Marble'
  • Introduced — Aquarium Plants Factory®, 2024
  • Placement — Midground, attached to wood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 3–5 in
  • Growth rate — Very slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced. Variegated leaves carry far less chlorophyll and are much less forgiving than green Anubias
  • Light — Low to medium. Steady, moderate light — not intense
  • CO₂ — Not required, though it helps a plant this slow
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5. Stability matters more than any specific value
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower’s Notes

  • White tissue does no photosynthesis. A heavily marbled plant runs on a fraction of the energy a green Anubias makes, so it grows slower, recovers slower, and has far less margin for a bad week. This is why it is Advanced despite being an Anubias.
  • It can revert. Under poor conditions the plant may start pushing plain green leaves to compensate for lost pigment. Once it reverts, the marbling does not usually come back on those leaves.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Glue or tie it to wood or stone; buried rhizomes rot.
  • Keep light moderate and consistent. White leaf tissue burns and attracts algae faster than green tissue does.
  • Every plant is genuinely unique — the plant you receive will not match the photograph, by nature of the cultivar.

Want to go deeper? Read our Anubias Panda Marble care guide or our complete Anubias Care Guide.

products.title: Echinodorus Martii
products.body_html:
A sword with texture instead of just size. Echinodorus martii grows broad, arching leaves with deeply ruffled edges that catch light along every wave — where a standard Amazon Sword gives you a smooth green fountain, this gives you a crinkled one. It grows large, so it wants a tank with room.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose bare-root plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 1–2 individual bare-root plants
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 1–2 plants bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 1–2 plants rooted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Martii Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus martii
  • Also known as — Echinodorus major, Ruffled Amazon Sword
  • Origin — South America
  • Placement — Midground to background; centrepiece in larger tanks
  • Mature height — 10–16 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Not required, though it drives larger leaves
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — nutrient substrate and root tabs

  • Give it space before you buy it. Mature leaves arch wide as well as tall, so one plant occupies a lot of a 20-gallon tank. In a nano it will simply outgrow the glass.
  • Feed at the roots. Swords take most of their nutrition from the substrate — root tabs under the crown do more than any liquid dosing.
  • Plant the crown at substrate level. Burying it rots the plant.
  • Expect the first leaves to melt as it converts from emersed nursery growth. The second flush is the ruffled submerged form.
  • It propagates from flower stalks, not runners. A mature plant sends up an inflorescence carrying plantlets along its length; let each root, then cut it free and plant it separately.

products.title: Amazon Sword Mother Plant
products.body_html:
Want a centrepiece today rather than in a year? The Amazon Sword Mother Plant is a mature XL specimen — 13 inches or more — that fills a background the moment it goes in. Swords are slow, so buying one already grown is the only way to skip the wait.

What You’ll Receive

  • Bare-root plants | Approx. 1-2 loose plants with root
  • Bunched plants | Approx. 1-2 plants with root, bundled with foam, and lead weight
  • Potted plants | Approx. 1-2 plants with root, potted with net pot and Rockwool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Amazon Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus bleheri
  • Also known as — Echinodorus grisebachii 'Bleherae'
  • Placement — Background or centrepiece
  • Mature height — 16–24 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — root tabs are essential in inert gravel
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed

Grower’s Notes

  • Give it a tank with real depth. A plant this size in a shallow aquarium grows into the lid, bends over and shades everything around it. 29 gallons is a sensible minimum.
  • Plant the crown at the substrate line, never below it. A buried crown rots, and that is how most newly planted swords are lost.
  • Root tabs are not optional. Swords feed almost entirely through their roots, and liquid fertiliser does very little for them. Small pale new leaves means root nutrition, nine times out of ten.

Let each plantlet develop three or four leaves and visible roots, then cut it free and plant it — a mother plant this size will produce them.

products.title: Amazon Frogbit
products.body_html:
Fighting algae or want cover for fry and shrimp? Amazon Frogbit does both at once. Round, spongy leaves sit on the surface while long hair-like roots trail down into the water column — stripping the nitrate algae wants, shading the tank below, and giving shrimplets somewhere to hide.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a small portion – Approx. 2–3 individual plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Amazon Frogbit
  • Scientific name — Limnobium laevigatum
  • Placement — Floating on the surface
  • Mature height — Floats; roots trail several inches down
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner. One of the easiest plants you can buy
  • Light — Low to medium is plenty; it sits closest to the light already
  • CO₂ — Not required. It takes carbon straight from the air
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Feeding — Water column
  • Propagation — Runners; daughter plants appear on their own

Grower’s Notes

  • Keep the leaf tops dry. Water sitting on the leaves makes them yellow and rot, so aim filter outflow below the surface and skip the airstone underneath it.
  • Leave an air gap under the lid. Condensation dripping back down does exactly the same damage as spray.
  • Thin it every week or two. It doubles fast, and a solid mat of frogbit will shade out every plant beneath it — half to two-thirds surface cover is a sensible target.
  • Yellowing leaves usually mean iron or micronutrients, not light. Floating plants feed entirely from the water column and are the first to show a deficiency.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference; leaf size and root length vary with lighting and nutrient availability. Not suitable for tanks with strong surface agitation or high flow.
  • Some aquatic plants are restricted in certain U.S. states — check before ordering, and never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

Known for its round, green leaves that float gracefully on the water’s surface, Amazon Frogbit adds natural beauty and provides shade and shelter for fish. Its long, dangling roots not only enhance the aesthetic of your aquascape but also help improve water quality by absorbing excess nutrients.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Lucens
products.body_html:
Want a Crypt small enough for the foreground? Cryptocoryne lucens stays around 2–4 inches with slim, grass-like leaves — far narrower than the wendtii types most people start with — and spreads by runners into a low, dense group. It does that in low light, without CO₂. These are young plants grown in a controlled laboratory environment, so they arrive clean.

What You’ll Receive

  • Small Bare-root: 1 loose, small bare-root plant with 6+ leaves
  • Potted Plant: 1 plant with 6+ leaves, planted in rockwool inside a net pot
  • Young plants grown in a controlled laboratory environment (ex-vitro), offering a clean, pest-free start

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Crypt Lucens
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne lucens
  • Also known as — Cryptocoryne × willisii 'Lucens'
  • Origin — Sri Lanka
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Shipped size — Small plant, 6+ leaves
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Suits — 5 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Hard water suits it, as it does most Crypts
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

Care

Grower’s Notes

  • Fish generally leave it alone. Crinum foliage is tough and unpalatable, which makes this one of the few realistic plants for cichlid tanks, goldfish tanks and anywhere else that shreds normal planting.

  • Be patient. It is slow to establish and may sit for weeks doing nothing, then grow steadily for years. It is a long-term plant, not a quick fill.
  • Don't move it once planted. Crinum resents disturbance and sulks after relocation, sometimes for months.

products.title: Water Hyacinth
products.body_html:
The floater that flowers. Eichhornia crassipes holds itself up on inflated, spongy leaf stalks, sends a trailing curtain of dark roots into the water, and — given enough sun — throws up spikes of lavender-blue flowers with a yellow eye. Few pond plants strip nutrients from water as fast.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as fresh, healthy Water Hyacinth plants carefully inspected before shipping:

  • Sold as a portion with 2-3 leaf
  • Beautiful flower when established

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Water Hyacinth
  • Scientific name — Eichhornia crassipes
  • Placement — Free-floating
  • Mature height — 4–8 in above the surface
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high. Six or more hours of direct sun for flowers
  • CO₂ — Not required. It takes CO₂ from the air
  • Water — 68–85°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required
  • Growth habit — True aquatic, free-floating
  • Propagation — Runners — daughter plants form on side stolons

Grower’s Notes

  • This is a pond plant, not an aquarium plant. It needs full sun and room to sit above the surface. Under an aquarium light in a covered tank it stretches, rots and disappoints — outdoors it thrives.
  • Nutrient export is its real job. A mat of Water Hyacinth pulls nitrate and phosphate out fast, which is why it clears green pond water so effectively.
  • The root curtain is prime spawning cover for goldfish and koi, and a nursery for fry.
  • Thin it every couple of weeks in summer. Left alone it doubles quickly and can seal a pond surface.
  • Flowering needs sun and maturity — young plants leaf first and bloom later in the season.

Notes

  • Water Hyacinth grows quickly in warm conditions. Manage growth responsibly and thin regularly.
  • Never release pond plants into natural waterways.

What You'll Receive

Plant Profile

  • Pinholes in the leaves mean potassium. Pinnatifida is the plant in most tanks that shows a potassium shortfall first — small holes appear in older leaves and spread. Dosing potassium clears it within a few weeks; it is not a pest or a disease.

Gratiola viscidula, commonly known as Hedge Hyssop, is a distinctive North American native that has quickly gained attention in the aquarium hobby for its rare and “thorny” submerged appearance. Naturally found in wetland areas, pond margins, and stream edges, this hardy species is adaptable and can thrive fully submerged for extended periods. Its compact, multi-stemmed form makes it a perfect choice for adding texture and contrast to aquascapes.

When provided with good lighting, Gratiola viscidula can be trimmed low to create a dense, carpet-like effect, or allowed to branch and fill in as a lush midground accent. Its stems, approximately 1–2 cm wide, can reach over 10 cm tall, developing into a dense display of intricate foliage. In nature, it produces charming white tubular flowers with yellow centers during summer and fall.

Now available in our premium Vitro Culture® 4-inch bag, each portion yields many healthy plantlets grown in a sterile environment—100% free of snails, algae, pathogens, and pesticides—making it safe for shrimp tanks and sensitive aquariums.

products.title: Java Fern Black Forest
products.body_html:
Dark, almost black-green leaves with a heavily textured surface, growing dense rather than open. Leptochilus pteropus 'Black Forest' is the Java Fern to reach for when a scape needs shadow and mass at the back — and it asks for nothing more than the plain green form does.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose bare-root plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Bare-root Plants: Approximately 6+ leaf portion, loose rhizome
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 6+ leaf portion bundled with foam and plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 6+ leaf portion, potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Black Forest Java Fern
  • Scientific name — Leptochilus pteropus 'Black Forest' (syn. Microsorum pteropus)
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species ranges across Java, Malaysia, Thailand, northeast India and southern China
  • Placement — Midground to background, attached to driftwood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 8-12 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5, soft to moderately hard
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte — attach the rhizome to hardscape and never bury it.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; grows emersed as well as submersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division, plus plantlets from mature leaves

Grower's Notes

  • Dark plants need light behind them. Against black substrate and dark wood this variety vanishes. Set it where pale sand, light stone or bright green foliage sits behind or beside it and the depth of colour becomes the point.
  • It grows dense, so it needs space. Unlike the open, upright plain form, Black Forest fills in. Give it more room on the hardscape than you think it needs, or the inner leaves shade themselves and thin out.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots may go into substrate; the thick horizontal stem must stay in open water or it rots — the usual way a Java Fern is lost.
  • Black spots on old leaves are baby plants, not disease. Leave a spotted leaf in place until each plantlet has roots and two or three leaves, then detach and attach it elsewhere. This is how one plant becomes a wall of them.
  • Expect a change of leaf. We grow this emersed, so some arriving fronds will die back as it converts to submerged growth. That is the plant working, not failing.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Java Fern Care Guide.

Notes

Photos are sample representations. Actual plants may vary in size, shape, or coloration. Unless otherwise specified, we do not guarantee plants are free of pests, pesticides, or exclusively submerged-grown.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Lutea Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
An earthy Crypt that stays small. Cryptocoryne lutea grows narrow, slightly wavy leaves in olive-green to brown on a compact upright rosette — muted, natural tones that sit well against driftwood and stone rather than competing with them. Native to Sri Lanka and one of the more reliable species in the genus. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You’ll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing healthy Cryptocoryne lutea plantlets—ready to rinse, acclimate, and plant in your aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Crypt Lutea
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne lutea
  • Origin — Sri Lanka
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Intense light is not needed
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Hard water suits it, as it does most Crypts
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Muted is the point. Bright green and red plants fight each other for attention. Lutea's olive-brown tones do the opposite — they recede and make hardscape and coloured plants read more strongly. Useful in biotope and nature-style layouts.
  • Expect melt after planting. Crypts drop their leaves on a change of conditions and rebuild from the roots over two to four weeks. Leave them alone.
  • Place it once. Every move triggers another melt.
  • It spreads slowly by runners — give it a season and one plant becomes a small group.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before planting or it clouds water and feeds algae early on.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Cryptocoryne Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are sample representations. Actual leaf colour and size may vary depending on lighting, nutrients, and aquarium conditions. Some melting may occur when transitioning from tissue culture to submerged growth, followed by regrowth under stable conditions.

products.title: Echinodorus Ozelot Red
products.body_html:
Echinodorus 'Ozelot Red' is the spotted sword. Deep red-brown new leaves carry darker blotches that stay visible as the leaf matures toward green — a marbled pattern rather than a solid colour, on a rosette compact enough for a mid-sized tank.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a potted plant with roots developed
  • Beautiful, marble, compact sword plant
  • Rare, eye-catching colors sword plant

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ozelot Red Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus 'Ozelot Red'
  • Also known as — Red Ozelot Amazon Sword, Echinodorus 'Ozelot'
  • Origin — Cultivated hybrid; parent species from South America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; this is a root feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on flower stalks

Grower's Notes

  • The spots are the point, and they show best on new leaves. Emerging foliage comes through red-brown with dark blotches; as it matures the background greens and the spots remain. A well-fed plant always has spotted new growth at the centre.
  • Root tabs are not optional. Swords take nearly all their nutrition from the substrate. In inert gravel with liquid dosing alone the spotting fades and growth stalls — which people mistake for a difficult plant rather than a hungry one.
  • Never bury the crown. Cover the roots and leave the growing point at substrate level. A buried crown rots from the centre and does not recover.
  • It propagates from flower stalks, not runners. A mature plant sends up an inflorescence carrying plantlets along its length; let each root and grow three or four leaves before cutting it free.
  • Give it clear space. At 10-16 inches with broad leaves it shades a wider area than the height suggests — treat it as a focal plant rather than a filler.

products.title: Anubias Petite White Panda | Small Vitro Culture Cup
products.body_html:
Heart-shaped leaves split between white and green. Anubias 'Petite White Panda' is among the rarest Anubias in the hobby and among the hardest to keep — the two facts are related. This is the small tissue culture cup, grown in our own lab in the USA.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as Tissue Culture Plants in 1 oz cup
  • APF premium product, grown in our lab in USA
  • One of the rarest Anubias species on the market

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Petite White Panda Anubias
  • Scientific name — Anubias barteri var. nana 'Petite White Panda'
  • Origin — Cultivated variegated form; the genus is native to West and Central Africa
  • Placement — Midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 1-3 inches
  • Growth rate — Very slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light scorches the white tissue and feeds algae.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Stability matters far more than any additive.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte — attach the rhizome to hardscape and never bury it.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • This is not an easy plant, and the reason is chlorophyll. White areas of the leaf cannot photosynthesise, so a heavily marked Panda runs on a fraction of the energy a green Anubias makes. Expect very slow growth, poor recovery from damage, and no ability to outgrow algae. It rewards a stable, well-run tank rather than a bright one.
  • It can revert. Under weak light or thin feeding the plant may start pushing plain green leaves. Remove them promptly — green growth photosynthesises better and will out-compete the marked tissue if left.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots can go into substrate; the rhizome cannot. Buried, it rots, and this plant will not recover from that.
  • Rinse the gel off with aquarium or dechlorinated water, not tap, before attaching.
  • Place one as a feature rather than several as a group. At this price and this size, a single well-lit-but-shaded specimen against dark hardscape does more than a scattered handful.

products.title: Willow Moss
products.body_html:
The moss for cold tanks. Fontinalis antipyretica — Willow Moss — comes from cool, clear streams across the Northern Hemisphere and prefers water between 60 and 75°F. In an unheated or lightly heated tank, where tropical mosses sulk, this one thrives — growing long, flowing, willow-like fronds off rock and driftwood.

  • Placement — Midground, attached to rock, driftwood or mesh

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Thrives in shade
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 60–75°F · pH 6.0–7.5. Note the ceiling — this is a cold-water moss
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — True aquatic. Does not grow emersed
  • Propagation — Fragmentation — divide and re-attach

Grower’s Notes

  • The temperature range is the reason to buy it. Most aquarium mosses want tropical warmth. Willow Moss wants 60–75°F — which makes it one of the very few mosses that works in a goldfish tank, an unheated room-temperature setup, or a coldwater biotope.
  • Above 78–80°F it thins and browns. In a tropical community tank, use Java Moss or Christmas Moss instead.
  • Tie or glue it thinly. Thick mats trap detritus and rot from underneath; a thin layer grows across the surface.
  • Flowing fronds give shrimp and fry excellent cover and a large surface for biofilm.
  • Arriving compressed and dark is normal. Rinse gently, place it in clean water, and colour returns within days.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete guide to Fontinalis antipyretica.

Notes

  • Live aquatic moss may appear slightly compressed or darker upon arrival due to shipping conditions. Simply rinse gently and place it in clean aquarium water; it will regain its vibrant colour and fullness within a few days.
  • Some aquatic plants are restricted in certain U.S. states — check before ordering, and never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Microsorum Pteropus Trident
products.body_html:
Want Java Fern with a finer silhouette? Trident splits each leaf into narrow forked fingers instead of a single broad blade — more movement, more detail, and it reads far lighter on hardscape than standard Java Fern. Same near-indestructible plant underneath.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Leptochilus pteropus 'Trident' cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in convenient planting formats:

Bare-root Plants: Approximately 3+ leaves per portion with loose rhizome and attached roots
Bunched Plants: Approximately 3+ leaves per portion bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement
Potted Plants: Approximately 3+ leaves per portion potted in a net pot with rockwool for stability and easy planting

Each portion may consist of individual leaves with separated rhizome sections, which is completely natural for this species. All pieces are viable and will continue to grow once placed in your aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Trident Java Fern
  • Scientific name — Leptochilus pteropus 'Trident' (formerly Microsorum pteropus)
  • Placement — Midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 6–10 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light means algae on slow-turning leaves
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape and feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division, plus plantlets on mature leaves

Grower’s Notes

  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie or glue it to wood or rock with the rhizome fully exposed — buried in substrate it rots, and this is how most Java Ferns are lost.
  • It clones itself. Small plantlets form along the edges and tips of mature leaves. Once one has a few leaves and visible roots, snap it off and attach it elsewhere — this is how a single portion becomes a wall of fern over a year.
  • Black spots on older leaves are usually plantlet sites or normal ageing, not disease. If whole leaves brown from the base, look at light and flow instead.
  • Trident grows faster and stays narrower than standard Java Fern, which makes it easier to use in smaller tanks without it swamping the hardscape.

products.body_html:

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Java Fern (Leptochilus pteropus) cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®.

Bare-root Portion: Approximately 6 individual leaves with some roots attached. Leaves may arrive separated, and rhizomes are not guaranteed to be connected. This is completely normal for Java Fern and makes it easier to attach each plant to driftwood, rocks, or other hardscape.

Unlike some sellers, we do not tie multiple rhizomes together with black cotton thread to make them appear as one clump, as this can restrict healthy growth, and increase the risk of rot over time.

  • 5 Pack: 5 individual bare-root portions (approximately 6 leaves per portion)
  • 10 Pack: 10 individual bare-root portions (approximately 6 leaves per portion)
  • 20 Pack: 20 individual bare-root portions (approximately 6 leaves per portion)

For best results, attach each leaf or rhizome section to driftwood, rocks, or other hardscape using cotton thread. New rhizomes and plantlets will naturally develop as the plant grows.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Java Fern
  • Scientific name — Leptochilus pteropus (syn. Microsorum pteropus)
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Midground, attached to driftwood, rock or décor
  • Mature height — 6-10 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required; it encourages faster growth and larger leaves but is not needed
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte — attach the rhizome to hardscape and never bury it.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; grows emersed as well as submersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division, plus plantlets from mature leaves

Grower's Notes

  • Buy coverage, do not wait for it. Java Fern adds only a few leaves a year. Twenty portions spread across a large piece of wood look established the day they go in; one portion never will.
  • Separated leaves are a feature, not damage. Each leaf with a scrap of rhizome and a root will grow into its own plant, and separate pieces are far easier to distribute across a hardscape than one bound clump. That is why we do not thread them together.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots may go into substrate; the green horizontal stem must stay in open water or it rots — the single most common way a Java Fern is killed.
  • Black spots on old leaves are baby plants, not disease. Leave a spotted leaf in place until each plantlet has roots and two or three leaves, then detach and attach it elsewhere. A bulk planting becomes self-propagating within a year.
  • Expect a change of leaf. We grow this emersed, so some arriving leaves will die back as the plants convert to submerged growth. That is the plant working, not failing.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Java Fern Care Guide.

Notes

Pictures are representative samples only. Live aquatic plants are natural products and may vary in size, color, and fullness depending on season and growing conditions. Java Fern is commonly grown emersed and may experience a normal transition period as it adapts to submerged aquarium conditions.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.body_html:
One Amazon Sword fills a corner. Twenty fill a wall. Echinodorus bleheri is the standard background plant of the hobby — broad ribbed green blades, no CO₂ needed, and tough enough for cichlid and community tanks. This is the bulk pack, for furnishing a large aquarium or a shop in one go.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Amazon Sword (Echinodorus bleheri) cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®.

Each bundle is rooted and secured with aquarium-safe foam and a plant weight, containing approximately 1–2 healthy plants per bunch.

  • 5 Pack: 5 rooted bunched plants (approximately 1–2 plants per bunch)
  • 10 Pack: 10 rooted bunched plants (approximately 1–2 plants per bunch)
  • 20 Pack: 20 rooted bunched plants (approximately 1–2 plants per bunch)

Simply remove the foam and plant weight before planting if desired, and place the roots into a nutrient-rich substrate while keeping the crown above the substrate surface.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Amazon Sword, also known as Broad Leaf Amazon Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus bleheri
  • Also known as — Echinodorus grisebachii 'Bleherae'
  • Origin — South America
  • Placement — Background
  • Mature height — 16-20 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner, provided you feed the roots
  • Light — Medium. It reaches full size without high-output lighting.
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required. Steady growth either way.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — root tabs are not optional in inert gravel.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on aerial floral stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Space them wider than you think. A mature Amazon Sword spreads a foot across. Twenty planted at four-inch spacing will shade each other out within a year — plant for the size they reach, not the size they arrive at, and use the spare plants elsewhere.
  • Bulk buying only pays if the substrate can feed them. Twenty heavy root feeders in inert gravel will all yellow together. Budget for root tabs across the whole planted area, or use aquasoil.
  • Give them depth. Three inches of substrate, crown set at the surface and never below. The root mass is substantial and a shallow bed stunts the whole planting.
  • Expect a transition. These are grown emersed, so some arriving leaves will die back as the plants convert to submerged growth. New leaves follow from the crown.
  • They propagate themselves. Settled plants throw tall floral stalks carrying plantlets. Leave each one attached until it has four or five leaves and its own roots, then cut it free — a bulk planting becomes self-replacing within a year.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Amazon Sword Care Guide.

Notes

Pictures are representative samples only. Live aquatic plants are natural products and may vary in size, color, and fullness depending on season and growing conditions. Amazon Sword is commonly grown emersed and may experience a normal transition period as it adapts to submerged aquarium conditions.

products.title: Red Tiger Lotus | Bulk Pack
products.body_html:
One hundred bulbs, priced for volume. Red Tiger Lotus (Nymphaea zenkeri) grows broad arrow-shaped leaves in deep red without CO₂ or high-output lighting — and at this quantity it becomes viable for pond planting, retail resale, or filling a large display. Bulbs are sold as-is: the sprout rate is high, but individual bulbs are not guaranteed.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Red Tiger Lotus, Tiger Lotus
  • Scientific name — Nymphaea zenkeri 'Red'
  • Plant type — Bulb / tuber
  • Placement — Background or centrepiece; also suits ponds
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — High. Light intensity is what brings out the red and the mottling
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — True aquatic. This plant cannot be grown emersed

Grower's Notes

  • Plan for losses and it's still the cheaper route. At bulk pricing, even a proportion of duds costs less per grown plant than buying sprouted bulbs individually — which is the whole reason this pack exists.

  • Root tabs are not optional. In inert gravel these stay small and green instead of colouring up.

products.body_html:
The moss that grows upward. Taxiphyllum sp. 'Flame' sends tight, twisting shoots vertically rather than sprawling sideways — the effect is a cluster of dark green flames rising off the hardscape. No other aquarium moss does this, which is why it's used where a moss needs to have a shape rather than just cover something. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Flame Moss, Fire Moss
  • Scientific name — Taxiphyllum sp. 'Flame'
  • Also known as — Vesicularia sp. 'Flame', Asian Flame Moss

products.body_html:
Achilles Black is one of the darkest Bucephalandra varieties in the trade — near-black green leaves that catch blue when light strikes them at an angle. Like every Buce it grows slowly on wood or rock and asks for very little, which is exactly why collectors keep it.

What You'll Receive

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Achilles Black Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Achilles Black'

  • Origin — Borneo, Indonesia

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium

  • Expect roughly an inch of growth per year. Bucephalandra is one of the slowest plants sold. Most arrive around 2-3 inches and stay close to that for a long time — which is why it holds a scape's composition without trimming.
  • Never bury the rhizome. The horizontal stem must sit in open water, tied or glued to a surface. Buried, it rots, and a plant this slow does not grow back from it in a season.
  • Dark varieties need low light, not none. Strong lighting bleaches the near-black tone toward green and invites algae onto leaves the plant cannot replace quickly. Low to medium light keeps it dark.
  • Look at it from the side. The blue iridescence on dark Buce only shows at an angle. Mounted flat on the substrate and viewed from above, it just reads as a dark green plant.

products.body_html:
Round leaves held up like small umbrellas. Hydrocotyle verticillata joins each leaf to its stalk at the centre rather than the edge, so the foliage stands upright on thin stems instead of trailing flat — a shape nothing else in a planted tank produces. This is the sterile tissue culture version.

  • Origin — The Americas

  • Bare stalks with few leaves means not enough light. Under weak lighting the stems stretch upward and the umbrella leaves thin out. Raise the intensity or move it forward rather than dosing more fertiliser.

Grower’s Notes

  • Flow is the difference between thriving and sulking. Bolbitis evolved in fast water and takes much of its nutrition from the passing current. Place it in a stagnant corner and it stalls; place it in the outflow and it thrives.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie or glue it to wood or rock — buried rhizomes rot.
  • Rinse all nutrient gel off before attaching, separate into portions, and expect a stall of several weeks while it converts to submerged growth. That pause is normal for the genus.
  • Slow growth plus translucent fronds means algae shows clearly. Keep light moderate and the tank balanced.
  • Divide the rhizome into sections with several fronds each once it has bulked up.

Notes

  • Pictures are for reference only and may not represent the exact plants you will receive. Tissue Culture plants are grown in sterile laboratory conditions and are 100% snail-free, algae-free, duckweed-free, and pest-free. Plant size, number of leaves, and clump size may vary naturally depending on the stage of growth at the time of harvest.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Java Fern Lionfish
products.body_html:
Java Fern, deeply cut. Leptochilus pteropus 'Lionfish' splits each leaf into narrow, finely dissected lobes that fan out and drift in the current like the fins the variety is named after. It is the most intricate leaf shape in the Java Fern range — and it asks for exactly as little as the plain form does.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Leptochilus pteropus ‘Lionfish’ cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in convenient planting formats:

  • Bare-root Plants: Approximately 3+ leaf portion, loose rhizome
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 3+ leaf portion bundled with foam and plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 3+ leaf portion, potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Lionfish Java Fern
  • Scientific name — Leptochilus pteropus 'Lionfish' (syn. Microsorum pteropus)
  • Placement — Midground, attached to driftwood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 6–10 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division, plus plantlets from mature leaves

Grower’s Notes

  • Put it in the flow. The dissected leaves are built to move — in still water Lionfish just looks like a ragged Java Fern, but in a current it drifts constantly and earns its name. Place it where the filter return reaches.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie or glue it to wood or stone; buried rhizomes rot.
  • Black spots on older leaves are usually plantlets forming, not disease. Let them root, then detach and attach elsewhere.
  • Intricate leaves collect detritus in low-flow corners — another reason to give it movement.
  • Pair with Broad Leaf for maximum contrast: identical care, opposite silhouettes.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Java Fern Care Guide.

Notes

  • Appearance may vary slightly due to natural growth conditions. As an epiphytic plant, the rhizome should not be buried in substrate to prevent rot. Minor leaf melt may occur during transition but new growth will adapt to your aquarium.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

featured_image.alt: Microsorum pteropus 'Lionfish,' also recognized by its common name, the Java Fern Lionfish, is a captivating and distinctive aquatic plant that has gained popularity among aquarium enthusiasts. This unique variant of the widely-admired Java Fern, Microsorum pteropus, is renowned for its striking and intricate leaf structure, which closely resembles the graceful fins of a lionfish, hence its name.

products.title: Giant Water Snowflake
products.body_html:
Round green pads floating on the surface with small white fringed flowers held just above them — Nymphoides indica gives a pond look inside an aquarium. Leaves can exceed four inches across, which makes this one of the larger plants in the Water Snowflake group.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Giant Water Snowflake (Nymphoides indica) plants cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®.

Available in convenient pack sizes:

  • Pack 1 Plant: Small fresh-cut plant with approximately 1 leaves (no roots or flowers).
  • Pack 5 Plants: Five small fresh-cut plants with approximately 1 leaves each (no roots or flowers).
  • Pack 10 Plants: Ten small fresh-cut plants with approximately 1 leaves each (no roots or flowers).

Plants are shipped as small fresh-cut plants. Once placed in the aquarium or pond, they will continue to grow and develop additional floating leaves under suitable conditions.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Giant Water Snowflake
  • Scientific name — Nymphoides indica
  • Also known as — Water Snowflake, Banana Plant relative; family Menyanthaceae
  • Origin — Tropical Asia, Africa and Australia
  • Placement — Floating, or rooted in substrate with leaves reaching the surface
  • Leaf size — Round pads over 4 inches across when mature
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Optional; roots into soil or floats free
  • Growth habit — True aquatic with floating leaves
  • Propagation — Runners and plantlets at the leaf nodes

Grower's Notes

  • It arrives as a leaf, not a plant. Each pack is a small fresh-cut piece with about one leaf and no roots. Float it and it grows its own roots and further pads over the following weeks — the mature look in the photos takes a couple of months.
  • Let it float rather than planting it. Free-floating leaves get direct light and grow largest. Rooted in substrate it still works, but the pads stay smaller and take longer.
  • Plan for the shade it casts. Four-inch pads on the surface block a lot of light. That is useful over shy fish or to suppress algae, but anything light-hungry underneath will suffer.
  • Flowers need maturity and stability. The white fringed blooms appear on established plants in good conditions — not on a freshly shipped cutting.
  • It multiplies from the leaf nodes. New plantlets form where leaf meets stem; detach them once they have their own roots and you have free stock.

Notes

  • Appearance, size, and coloration may vary depending on growing conditions and season. Plants may arrive in their emersed (farm-grown) form and will transition to their submerged aquarium form after acclimation.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Bucephalandra Red Phantom Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Red Phantom comes from the Lamandau region of Borneo. Grown above water it shows green leaves on red stems — the stem colour is the point of the variety. This is the tissue-culture format: sterile, snail-free, four plantlets per bag.

What You'll Receive

  • Common name — Red Phantom Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Red Phantom'
  • Also known as — Bucep Red Phantom, Buce Red Phantom
  • Origin — Lamandau, Borneo
