products.title: Nymphaea Golden West | Pink Tropical Water Lily
products.body_html:
Nymphaea 'Golden West' is a captivating tropical water lily hybridized by Martin E. Randig in 1936. This medium-sized aquatic plant is renowned for its profuse flowering and beautiful autumn-pink blooms that add a vibrant touch to any pond or water garden.

Key Features:

  • Vibrant Pink Blooms: The flowers of Nymphaea 'Golden West' exhibit a charming autumn-pink color, adding a stunning visual appeal to your water garden. Each flower is cup-shaped to star-shaped, enhancing its aesthetic charm.
  • Distinctive Foliage: The lily features green leaves with new growth emerging mottled with red, maturing to a lush green. These leaves float gracefully on the water’s surface, providing a beautiful backdrop for the flowers.

Optimal Conditions:

  • Sunlight: Thrives in full sun, requiring at least 6 hours of direct sunlight daily for optimal blooming.
  • Water Depth: Best planted at a depth of 12 to 36 inches (30-90 cm) in still or slow-moving water.
  • Soil Type: Prefers heavy clay or loam soils, typically planted in containers submerged in the pond for best results.

Benefits:

  • Aesthetic Appeal: Enhances the visual appeal of any pond with its vibrant pink flowers and lush green foliage.
  • Wildlife Attraction: Attracts beneficial wildlife such as bees and dragonflies, contributing to a healthy pond ecosystem.
  • Profuse Bloomer: Known for its abundant flowering, ensuring a long-lasting display of color throughout the growing season.

Care and Maintenance:

  • Fertilization: Regular fertilization during the growing season with aquatic plant fertilizer promotes healthy growth and abundant blooming.
  • Pruning: Remove yellowing leaves and spent flowers to encourage new growth and maintain plant health.
  • Winter Care: As a tropical water lily, it requires special care in colder climates. In regions with cold winters, it is best to lift the plant and store it in a warm, frost-free area until spring.

Conclusion:

Nymphaea 'Golden West' is an exceptional tropical water lily that brings vibrant color and elegance to any pond or water garden. Its stunning autumn-pink flowers, distinctive foliage, and ease of care make it an excellent choice for enhancing your aquatic landscape. Add the enchanting Nymphaea 'Golden West' to your pond today and enjoy the continuous beauty it brings to your water garden environment.

  • You will get 1 young and freshly harvested water lily tuber
  • All of our water lilies tubers/rhizomes have been inspected before ship out and guaranteed they are viable and perfect to grow in a proper pond environment

PLANTING INSTRUCTIONS FOR WATER LILY

 

There are two main types of water lilies, tropical and hardy. The differences between tropical and hardy water lilies are a growing habit. Tropical water lilies don't do well in winter. Hardy water lilies, on the other hand, can tolerate the cold. Tropical water lilies tubers must be removed from the pond and stored in moist conditions to come back in the future years. In warm climates, they can remain in the pond.

products.title: Nymphaea Tina | Violet Tropical Water Lily
products.body_html:
Nymphaea 'Tina' is a tropical day-bloomer that does something most lilies do not — it grows new plants on its own leaves. Deep violet-purple cup-shaped flowers with golden centres, a genuine sweet scent, and pads that emerge bronze before turning green.

What You'll Receive

You will receive 1 young, freshly harvested waterlily tuber.

  • All tubers/rhizomes are carefully inspected before shipping and guaranteed viable, healthy, and ready to grow in a proper pond environment.
  • Note: The images shown are sample representations. The actual product you receive may not be identical, as live plants vary in size and stage.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Tina Tropical Water Lily
  • Scientific name — Nymphaea 'Tina'
  • Type — Tropical, day-blooming, viviparous
  • Flower — Cup-shaped violet-purple with golden-yellow centres, lightly fragrant
  • Origin — Cultivated hybrid
  • Placement — Centrepiece in a pond or water garden
  • Mature height — 12-24 inches
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Sunlight — Full sun, 6+ hours daily
  • Planting depth — 12-24 inches from soil surface to water surface
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Soil — Heavy clay or loam, capped with gravel; this is a root feeder
  • Feeding — Aquatic fertiliser tablets monthly through the growing season
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • It also propagates off its own pads. Beyond dividing the rhizome, this viviparous cultivar grows a small plantlet at the centre of a mature leaf. Let it develop roots and two or three leaves of its own, then cut the pad free and pot it — one tuber becomes several plants in a season.
  • Tropical means it will not overwinter outdoors in a cold region. The tuber has to be lifted and stored in moist conditions over winter unless you are in a warm climate. Hardy lilies stay in the pond; this one does not.
  • Six hours of direct sun is the requirement. Shade is the usual reason a lily makes plenty of pads and few flowers.
  • Plant the tuber with the crown clear of the soil. Set it upright with the growing tip above the soil line, then cap with gravel. Buried crowns rot.
  • The flowers stand above the water. Unlike hardy lilies, which float their blooms, tropicals hold theirs on stems clear of the surface — which is why the scent actually reaches you.

Planting Instructions for Water Lily

There are two main types of water lilies, tropical and hardy. The differences between tropical and hardy water lilies are a growing habit. Tropical water lilies don't do well in winter. Hardy water lilies, on the other hand, can tolerate the cold. Tropical water lilies tubers must be removed from the pond and stored in moist conditions to come back in the future years. In warm climates, they can remain in the pond.

Notes

  • All water lilies are shipped bare-root (as tubers) and should be planted immediately upon arrival for best results. Bloom and leaf color, size, and shape may vary slightly depending on lighting, water quality, and plant maturity.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Alternanthera Ficoidea Rainbow
products.body_html:
Read this first: this is not a true aquatic plant. Alternanthera ficoidea 'Rainbow' is a garden and terrarium plant. Kept underwater it holds its red, yellow and green variegation for several months and then needs a spell of emersed growth to recover. Bought with that in mind, few plants carry this much colour.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as loose Fresh-cut Plants, Bunched plants, or Potted plants
  • Fresh-cut plants | approx. 5 stems, loose fresh-cut plants without root
  • Bunched plants | approx. 5 fresh-cut plants without root bundle with foam, and plant's weight
  • Potted plants | approx. 5 fresh-cut plants potted with net pot and rock wool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Rainbow Alternanthera
  • Scientific name — Alternanthera ficoidea 'Rainbow'
  • Also known as — Rainbow Joseph's Coat
  • True aquatic — No
  • Best suited to — Terrarium, vivarium, riparium, paludarium or bog planting
  • Origin — South America; widely cultivated as a garden plant
  • Placement — Midground
  • Shipped size — Approx. 5 fresh-cut stems, roughly 3-6 inches
  • Mature height — 4-8 inches
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up, or any humid terrarium
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended when submerged
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; also feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Non-aquatic; submerged use is temporary, emersed growth is permanent
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • This is not a true aquatic plant, and we would rather say so. Submerged it survives and even puts on a few inches over several months, but it does not grow indefinitely underwater. Plan to rotate it out to a humid emersed setup to recover, or treat it as a seasonal accent.
  • It is at its best above the waterline. In a riparium, paludarium, vivarium or bog planting with consistently wet soil and high humidity, the red-yellow-green variegation is far stronger and the plant grows without a time limit.
  • Light drives the colour range. Under moderate light the foliage leans green. Strong light — bright LED or partial sun emersed — is what brings out the reds and yellows that give it the name.
  • Take cuttings before it declines. Root fresh tops in wet soil while the parent is still strong. Waiting until the submerged plant fades usually means the cuttings are too weak to take.
  • Want permanent colour underwater? Alternanthera reineckii is the same genus, fully submersible, and stays red indefinitely.

products.title: Rotala Macrandra
products.body_html:
The plant that separates good tanks from great ones. Rotala macrandra carries the largest leaves in the genus — broad, soft and translucent — in a red that runs from rose to deep crimson. It is also the least forgiving Rotala we sell. Light, CO₂ and iron all have to be right at the same time, and the plant tells you immediately when one of them slips.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as emerged fresh-cut plants without root
  • Fresh-cut plants | approx. 6 loose fresh-cut plants
  • Bunched plants | approx. 6 fresh-cut plants bundle with foam and plant weight
  • Potted plants | approx. 6 fresh-cut plants potted with net pot and rock wool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Rotala Macrandra
  • Scientific name — Rotala macrandra
  • Also known as — Giant Red Rotala, Rotala Rose
  • Origin — India
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems, roughly 4-8 in
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High. Below that the stems stretch, the lower leaves drop and the red fades to a washed bronze
  • CO₂ — Required. This is the one Rotala where injection is not optional in practice
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Soft water gives the best colour
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich substrate plus water column dosing; iron in particular drives the red
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower's Notes

  • The leaves are thin enough to be an algae magnet. Soft, broad foliage collects detritus wherever flow is weak, and algae follow within days. Steady circulation through the group matters as much as the lighting does.
  • Lean nitrate is what makes it red. Fed heavily it grows green and leafy no matter how strong the light — hold iron and micros steady while keeping nitrate modest.
  • Trim before it reaches the surface. Once the tops shade the stems beneath, the lower half strips bare and does not recover.
  • Replant the tops and discard the old bases. Cuttings root and colour up faster than the stumps they came from.
  • If this proves too demanding, Rotala macrandra 'Green' has the same soft, round-leaved habit without the pigment demand — no iron chase, no colour to lose.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Rotala Care Guide.

products.title: Anubias Golden (Small Size)
products.body_html:
Bright yellow-green leaves in a genus that is otherwise uniformly dark. Anubias Golden pushes new growth in a golden-lime tone that deepens toward green as each leaf matures. This is the young grade — small now, growing into full size in your tank.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as young, miniature size Anubias Golden
  • Sustainable growth Anubias species
  • Fresh and clean, grow direct from our high technology lab farm
  • Young plants grow in a controlled laboratory environment

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Golden Anubias (Small)
  • Scientific name — Anubias barteri 'Golden'
  • Also known as — Anubias Golden Nana
  • Origin — Cultivated variety; the genus is native to West and Central Africa
  • Placement — Midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Shade suits it; strong light means algae on slow-turning leaves.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Occasional liquid fertiliser deepens the colour.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte — attach the rhizome to wood or stone and never bury it.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • The gold is new growth, not variegation. Each leaf emerges pale golden-lime and darkens with age, so the colour sits at the growing tip. That also means it is normally pigmented — no harder to grow than any other Anubias.
  • Place it against something dark. The pale new growth is the whole point and it disappears against light sand or pale stone. Dark wood or black lava rock is where it earns its price.
  • Buy small when you need several. Anubias adds roughly a leaf a month at any size, so a group bought young costs a fraction and catches up within a year.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots can go into substrate; the rhizome cannot. Buried, it rots.
  • Lab-grown means no snails, no algae and no pesticide residue — safe for a shrimp tank with no quarantine.

products.title: Helanthium Quadricostatus (Echinodorus) Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Helanthium quadricostatus is the broad-leaved chain sword — wider blades than the Tenellum forms, spreading by runner into a low green band across the front of a tank. No CO₂, medium light, and it does the work itself once rooted.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a Tissue Culture package with vitamin liquid/gel
  • Package size: Approx. 4 inches
  • Sustainable growth aquarium plants species
  • Great value! Nice specimen!
  • Tissue Culture Technology | 100% Free from Snail, Algae, Pathogen, and Bacteria plus Extended Shelf Life on all in Vitro Plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Broad Leaf Chain Sword
  • Scientific name — Helanthium quadricostatus
  • Also known as — Helanthium bolivianum 'Quadricostatus', Echinodorus quadricostatus, Bolivian Sword Plant
  • Origin — South America
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 4-8 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; this is a root feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower's Notes

  • Leave the runners attached until the daughter roots. Each runner sets a new rosette a few inches out. Cutting it free early stalls both plants; once it has its own roots it can be lifted and moved anywhere.
  • Broader blades than the other chain swords. If Tenellum has looked too grassy or too fine in your layout, this is the same habit at a heavier leaf — it reads as a plant rather than as turf.
  • Feed the roots, not the water. Chain swords take most of their nutrition from the substrate. Root tabs under the planting area matter far more than liquid dosing.
  • Height depends on light. Under medium light it stays low and spreads. In weak light it stretches taller and thinner reaching for the surface — the plant is fine, it is just growing to a different shape.
  • Thin it once a year. Left alone the rosettes crowd and the middle of the patch goes bare. Pulling every second plant and replanting it keeps the stand even.

products.title: Staurogyne Repens White Albino Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Staurogyne repens is one of the most reliable low carpeting plants in the hobby. The 'White Albino' form takes that familiar shape and strips almost all the green out of it, leaving pale ivory foliage that glows against dark substrate. Less chlorophyll means less energy, so it asks for considerably more than the standard form.

What You'll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing healthy Staurogyne Repens 'White Albino' plantlets—ready to rinse, acclimate, and plant with care.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — White Albino Staurogyne
  • Scientific name — Staurogyne repens 'White Albino'
  • Also known as — Staurogyne repens 'Variegated'
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species comes from the Rio Cristalino, Brazil
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 inches
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Medium. Note the ceiling — strong light bleaches pale tissue
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious creeping stem
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower's Notes

  • Pale tissue burns before green tissue does. Do not treat "needs light" as "needs more light". Medium intensity is the target — strong light bleaches the ivory leaves and algae takes hold on them long before it touches anything green in the tank.
  • Reverted green shoots will appear. Any pale sport can throw fully green growth, and green grows faster. Cut those stems out at the base as soon as you spot them or they will take over the group.
  • Feed the substrate. With reduced pigment the plant cannot afford an inefficient root zone. Aquasoil or root tabs under the planting area make the difference between slow and stalled.
  • Plant small portions, spaced out. Rinse the gel off and separate the culture into groups of two or three plantlets an inch apart. Dense clumps shade their own bases, which this plant recovers from poorly.
  • Want the same carpet without the difficulty? Standard Staurogyne repens is a Beginner plant with the same shape and growth habit — the albino form is a collector's plant, not a workhorse.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Staurogyne Repens Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos shown are sample representations. Actual plant appearance may vary depending on lighting, CO₂, and care. This albino variant is fragile and may melt if not given proper light and nutrients. Not recommended for beginners.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

This plant is typically offered in its emersed form, allowing it to adapt quickly to a variety of semi-aquatic and marginal aquatic environments. products.title: Cryptocoryne Flamingo
products.body_html:
The pink Crypt everyone wants and few keep. Cryptocoryne wendtii 'Pink Flamingo' carries pink and white variegation across the whole leaf — not a tint over green, but a genuine loss of chlorophyll. That is what makes the colour so striking and what makes the plant so slow and so unforgiving. Buy it knowing that.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as small Bare-root Plants or Potted plants
  • Bare-root plant | one small size, loose rooted plants
  • Potted plant | one rooted small size plant, potted with net pot and rockwool
  • Young plants grow in a controlled laboratory environment

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pink Flamingo Crypt
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne wendtii 'Pink Flamingo'
  • Also known as — Crypt Flamingo, Cryptocoryne Pink Panther
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Sri Lanka
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 3–5 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced. The variegation is why
  • Light — Medium to high. It needs more light than a green Crypt to make the same energy
  • CO₂ — Recommended. It holds colour and compact form far better with it
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Hard water suits it, as it does most Crypts
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Pink means less chlorophyll, which means less margin. A green Crypt survives neglect. Pink Flamingo doesn't — it grows slowly even at its best, so any setback costs months rather than weeks.
  • Expect it to melt after planting and rebuild from the roots over several weeks. That is normal for the genus and slower here than in green forms.
  • Place it once and leave it. Every move triggers another melt, and this plant recovers slowly.
  • Reversion happens. Under weak light or thin feeding it may push greener leaves — the plant compensating for lost pigment.
  • Want the colour with less risk? Cryptocoryne petchii 'Pink' is a beginner plant with a soft pink tone over green rather than true variegation.

products.body_html:

  • Keep it in low light to hold the compact form. Under brighter light it stretches and loses the tight habit you paid for.
  • Grown emersed at our nursery, which builds a strong rhizome. Expect a short transition as it converts to submerged growth.

  • Difficulty — Intermediate

  • Light decides whether it is yellow or just green. Under medium light the leaves lean pale green; stronger light brings out the golden tone and the orange-red edging. This is the one variable worth adjusting if the colour disappoints.

products.body_html:

products.body_html:
Growing a lotus from seed takes about a week to sprout and a season to flower, and the seed itself is the cheapest way into a plant that otherwise ships as an expensive tuber. This is a mixed lot — pink, white, yellow and multi-coloured varieties — so you find out what you have when it blooms.

What You'll Receive

  • Scientific Name: Nelumbo nucifera
  • Common Name: Lotus
  • Product Type: Mixed Lotus Seeds (Hardy and Tropical Varieties)
  • Light Requirement: Full Sun
  • Planting Medium: Heavy clay soil or aquatic planting media
  • Germination Time: 1–7 days after soaking
  • Ideal Use: Outdoor ponds, decorative water gardens, patio water containers

How to Grow Lotus Seeds

  • 1. Scarify the seed. Lotus seeds are oval with one pointed end and one rounded end. Do not file the pointed (embryo) end. Instead, gently file the rounded end until you see the white inner layer. This helps water enter the seed and encourages germination.
  • 2. Soak the seed. Place the scarified seed in a container of warm, clean water (around 75–85°F or 24–29°C). Change the water daily to keep it fresh.
  • 3. Sprouting. Within 1–7 days, the seed will swell and a sprout will emerge. Allow the sprout to grow 4–6 inches before planting.
  • 4. Transfer to soil. Plant the sprouted seed into a pot filled with heavy clay soil or aquatic planting media. Submerge the pot under 2–4 inches of water.
  • 5. Growing in water. Place the potted seedling in a sunny, warm location. As it matures, the lotus will send leaves above the water's surface and eventually produce stunning blooms.

Grower's Notes

  • Filing the wrong end kills the seed. The pointed end holds the embryo. File the rounded end only, and only until the white layer shows — going deeper damages what you are trying to germinate. This one step accounts for most failed lotus seeds.
  • Change the soaking water daily. Stale water fouls and the seed rots before it sprouts. Fresh warm water every day for the first week is the difference between a 1-7 day germination and nothing.
  • Do not plant the sprout too early. Wait until the shoot is four to six inches long. Planted shorter, it struggles to reach light through the water and stalls.
  • Lotus needs more sun than a water lily. Full sun all day is the target. In partial sun you will get leaves and no flowers, and lotus leaves are large enough to be worth growing on their own — but flowering needs the light.
  • Expect flowers in the second season. A seed-grown lotus spends its first year building a rhizome. That is normal and not a sign anything is wrong.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Guide on How to Grow Lotus Flowers from Seeds.

Notes

  • While our lotus seeds (Nelumbo nucifera) are selected for very high sprouting rates, we do not guarantee the flower color or that every seed will successfully grow. Flower coloration may vary naturally. Proper care, growing conditions, and patience are essential for best results.

products.body_html:
Nymphaea × daubenyana is an exquisite aquatic plant that brings a touch of elegance to ponds and water gardens. products.title: Nymphaea King of Siam | Blue Tropical Water Lily
products.body_html:
Nymphaea 'King of Siam' carries double deep purple-blue petals stacked into a full, layered bloom — a 1998 Thai hybrid of 'Larp Prasert' × 'Colorata' by Chaiyaphon Thamasuwan. It is a tropical lily, so it wants heat and sun and comes indoors for winter in a cold climate.

What You'll Receive

  • Shipped bare-root as a tuber, ready to plant on arrival

Plant Profile

  • Common name — King of Siam Blue Tropical Water Lily
  • Scientific name — Nymphaea 'King of Siam'
  • Also known as — Nymphaea 'King of the Blues', Nymphaea 'Chalong Kwan'
  • Type — Tropical, day-blooming; hybrid of 'Larp Prasert' × 'Colorata' (Chaiyaphon Thamasuwan, 1998)
  • Flower — Double deep purple-blue petals
  • Placement — Centrepiece in a pond or water garden
  • Mature height — 12-24 inches
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Sunlight — Full sun, at least 6 hours daily
  • Planting depth — 6-18 inches of water over the tuber
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5; still to slightly moving
  • Soil — Heavy clay or loam, capped with gravel; this is a root feeder
  • Feeding — Water lily fertiliser tablets through the growing season
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Tropical, not hardy — this decides your winter. The tuber must be lifted and stored in moist conditions over winter unless you are in a warm climate. If you cannot do that, buy a hardy lily instead; they stay in the pond and return on their own.
  • True blue-purple is rare in lilies. Most pond lilies run pink, red, white or yellow. The blue-purple line traces back to N. colorata, which is this plant's parent — that is where the colour comes from.
  • Warm water matters as much as sun. A shaded or spring-fed pond that stays cool will give you pads and very few flowers no matter how much fertiliser goes in.
  • Plant the tuber upright with the crown exposed. Set it in the centre of the pot with the growing point above the soil line, then cap with gravel. Buried crowns rot.
  • Start shallow and lower it. Begin where the first leaves reach the surface easily and move the pot deeper as it grows. Dropping a young tuber straight to full depth stalls it.

Planting Instructions for Water Lily

There are two main types of water lilies, tropical and hardy. The differences between tropical and hardy water lilies are a growing habit. Tropical water lilies don't do well in winter. Hardy water lilies, on the other hand, can tolerate the cold. Tropical water lilies tubers must be removed from the pond and stored in moist conditions to come back in the future years. In warm climates, they can remain in the pond.

Notes

  • All water lilies are shipped bare-root (as tubers) and should be planted immediately upon arrival for best results. Bloom and leaf color, size, and shape may vary slightly depending on lighting, water quality, and plant maturity.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Ludwigia Senegalensis
products.body_html:
Veins you can actually see. Ludwigia senegalensis runs a network of dark red veins across brick-red to orange leaves, so the pattern reads as detail rather than a flat block of colour — closer to a patterned houseplant than to the usual red stem plant. It is the most distinctive Ludwigia we carry, and the most demanding.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as loose Fresh-cut plants, Bunched plants, or Potted plants
  • Fresh-cut plants | Approx. 6 stems, loose fresh-cut stems without root
  • Bunched plants | Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems without root, bundled with foam, and lead weight
  • Potted plants | Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems without root, potted with net pot and rockwool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ludwigia Senegalensis
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia senegalensis
  • Also known as — Ludwigia sp. 'Guinea', Guinea Ludwigia
  • Origin — West Africa
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems, roughly 4-8 in
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Medium to high. The vein pattern and brick-red colour both depend on it
  • CO₂ — Recommended. In practice this plant rarely performs without it
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich substrate plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim side shoots and replant

Grower's Notes

  • Stability is the requirement, not any single value. Senegalensis punishes swings in CO₂, temperature and dosing more than it punishes any particular parameter being slightly off. A settled, mature tank suits it; a new one usually does not.
  • It throws multiple side shoots readily, so a few stems become a bush faster than most Ludwigia. Trim shoots off to propagate, or leave them for a dense red-orange mass.
  • The veining is what you are paying for, and it needs light to show. Under weak lighting the leaves stay plain green and the pattern disappears.
  • Plant stems separately with space between them. Crowded, the lower leaves shade out and the pattern is lost exactly where you would see it.
  • Frequently confused with Ludwigia glandulosa. They look similar but come from opposite sides of the Atlantic — glandulosa is North American, this is West African.

products.title: Mini Pellia / Mini Coral Moss
products.body_html:
Want texture nothing else in the hobby can give you? Mini Pellia grows in finely branched, deep green fronds that look like miniature coral — dense compact cushions rather than the loose strands of a true moss. It is a liverwort, and it is the detail plant serious aquascapers reach for.

What You’ll Receive

  • Loose Portion: Approximately 2" × 2"
  • Ready to Attach: Suitable for rocks, driftwood, mesh, or other aquarium décor

Portion size and density may vary slightly because this is a natural live plant.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mini Pellia, Mini Coral Moss, Mini Liverwort
  • Scientific name — Riccardia chamedryfolia
  • Plant type — Liverwort, not a true moss
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood, stone or mesh
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate. Not hard, but slow and unforgiving of neglect
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required, but it rewards CO₂ more than most mosses do
  • Water — Cooler is better; it thrives below about 75°F and struggles in warm tanks
  • Feeding — Water column
  • Propagation — Fragmentation; reattach healthy clippings

Grower’s Notes

  • Temperature is the deciding factor. Riccardia is a cool-water plant — in a tank running above 78°F it thins, browns and slowly gives up no matter how good the light and CO₂ are.
  • Flow matters more than light. The dense fronds trap detritus in still water and rot from the inside, so give it gentle, steady circulation.
  • Tie it on thin and flat. A thick clump smothers itself long before the surface fills in, and this plant is far too slow to recover from that.
  • It attaches slowly. Expect a couple of months before it grips hardscape properly — keep the thread or mesh on until it does.
  • Not to be confused with plain Pellia (Monosolenium tenerum), which is thicker, faster, more brittle and far more heat tolerant.

products.title: Limnophila Aromatica
products.body_html:
Limnophila aromatica is the same rice paddy herb sold in Vietnamese markets, grown underwater. Whorls of narrow leaves sit green on top and purple underneath, and the purple deepens as light intensity climbs. It grows fast enough to fill a background in weeks.

What You'll Receive

Enhance your aquarium with our versatile selection of high-quality aquatic plants, available in three convenient formats:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Includes approximately 6 loose, fresh-cut stems without roots. Perfect for flexible planting arrangements.
  • Fresh-Cut Bunched: Approximately 6 fresh-cut stems without roots, bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Fresh-Cut Potted: About 6 fresh-cut stems without roots, securely potted in a net pot with rockwool, ensuring stability and healthy growth.

Choose the format that best suits your aquascaping needs and create a vibrant, lush underwater environment with our premium aquatic plants.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Rice Paddy Herb
  • Scientific name — Limnophila aromatica
  • Also known as — Ambulia, ngò om, Vietnamese coriander of the rice fields
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 8-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs, plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • The purple lives on the underside of the leaf. Viewed from above the plant reads green; from the front, the whorls show violet. Planting it where you look across it rather than down at it is what shows the colour off.
  • The scent comes out of water, not in it. Emersed leaves smell strongly of citrus and cumin when crushed — it is a culinary herb in Vietnam. Submersed growth has little scent, so buy it for the colour and the texture.
  • Trim aggressively and it branches. Cutting the top third repeatedly turns a single stem into a dense bush. Left alone it grows straight to the surface and drops its lower leaves.
  • Iron and light together drive the colour. Medium light with steady micronutrient dosing produces the purple. Strong light without iron gives you a fast green plant instead.
  • Plant stems apart, not in a bundle. Six stems pushed in as one clump shade each other and rot at the base. Space them half an inch apart and let them fill in.

products.title: Vallisneria Nana
products.body_html:
Want the flowing Vallisneria look without a curtain that swallows your tank? Vallisneria nana has the thinnest leaf blade in the genus — roughly 1 mm wide. Fine dark green ribbons that move constantly with the flow, reading as texture rather than as a solid wall.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as loose fresh-cut plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual loose, bare-root plants
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Vallisneria Nana, also known as Narrow Leaf Eelgrass
  • Scientific name — Vallisneria nana
  • Also known as — Vallisneria gracilis
  • Origin — Australia
  • Placement — Background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 2-3 bare-root plants, roughly 6-12 in
  • Mature height — 20–30 in, longer in the wild
  • Leaf width — Approx. 1 mm — the narrowest Vallisneria
  • Suits — 20 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium is enough
  • CO₂ — Not required! One of the best background plants for a low-tech tank
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–8.0. Handles hard alkaline water better than most
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — root tabs are what drive the runners
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • A 1 mm blade changes how it reads. Jungle Val and Gigantea form solid green curtains. Nana at this width lets light and sightlines through, so you get movement and depth without blocking the back of the tank.
  • Plant the crown at the substrate line, never below it. A buried crown rots, and that is the usual reason a new Val fails in its first fortnight.
  • Don't trim the tops to control height. Cut Vallisneria leaves brown at the cut and stay that way — remove whole leaves at the base instead.
  • It feeds at the roots. In inert gravel it survives but barely spreads; root tabs are what turn three plants into a stand.
  • Still a tall plant at 20–30 inches, and longer in the wild. In a shallow tank it reaches the surface and trails along it.

Want the patterned version? See Vallisneria nana 'Striped', the same narrow blade with brown tiger striping.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Vallisneria Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference; height and leaf width vary with lighting and tank depth. Some melting on introduction is normal, with regrowth from the crown. Aquarium-safe and shrimp-safe.

products.title: Eleocharis Vivipara
products.body_html:
Hairgrass that goes up, not sideways. Eleocharis vivipara — Giant Hairgrass — grows long slender blades that sway in the current instead of carpeting the floor, and it propagates in an unusual way: baby plants form at the leaf tips rather than on runners. That's what vivipara means, and it's why this Eleocharis behaves nothing like the carpeting species.

What You’ll Receive

  • Bare-root plants | loose, bare-root portion
  • This type of Hairgrass will grow tall, perfect for background aquarium

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Vivipara Hairgrass
  • Scientific name — Eleocharis vivipara
  • Also known as — Giant Hairgrass, Tall Hairgrass, Umbrella Hairgrass
  • Origin — Southeastern United States
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Loose bare-root portion, shorter than mature height
  • Mature height — 6–12 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Daughter plantlets at the leaf tips; also splits at the base

Grower’s Notes

  • Don't buy this one for a carpet. Dwarf Hairgrass and Eleocharis mini spread by runners along the substrate. Vivipara grows upward and multiplies from its own leaf tips — you get a tall grassy stand, not a lawn.
  • Harvest the tip plantlets. Cut them off once they have a few blades and roots, and plant them; that's how one portion becomes a stand.
  • Feed at the roots. It draws most of its nutrition from the substrate, so root tabs matter more than liquid dosing.
  • Trim the tops if it reaches too high — cut blades keep growing from the base.
  • Separate the portion into small clumps before planting rather than sinking it as one mass; the clumps root faster.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Dwarf Hairgrass (Eleocharis) Care Guide.

products.title: Alternanthera Ficoidea 'Pink'
products.body_html:
Read this first: this is not a true aquatic plant. Alternanthera ficoidea 'Pink' is a terrarium, vivarium and bog plant with vivid pink foliage. Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate

  • Keep humidity high during the recovery phase — that's when it is most vulnerable.
  • Light drives the colour. In shade the pink fades toward green.

'Mini' spreads by runners, but the fastest route to a finished carpet is planting many small clumps close together rather than waiting for a few to fill the gaps.   • Split every clump before planting. A 1" x 1" clump divides into six or eight small tufts. Planted half an inch apart, those tufts close ranks far faster than the intact clump would spread — so the bulk pack effectively covers several times its own area.

products.title: Subwassertang Moss (Round Pellia)
products.body_html:
Want the look of moss without the maintenance? Subwassertang forms soft, translucent ruffled fronds that tangle into loose bushy clusters — and despite the name, it isn't a moss at all. It's the gametophyte stage of a fern, which is why it behaves so differently from anything else in the tank.

What You’ll Receive

  • Loose Portion: Includes a small, loose portion of Subwassertang Moss (approx. 2" x 2")
  • Ready to Use: Can be attached directly to your aquascaping elements with glue, thread, or simply tucked into crevices

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Subwassertang, Round Pellia, Loma Fern
  • Scientific name — Lomariopsis lineata
  • Plant type — Fern gametophyte (prothallus), not a true moss
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached or floating
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner. Tolerates a wide range of conditions
  • Light — Low to medium. It genuinely prefers shade
  • CO₂ — Not required! Denser with it, perfectly happy without
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Feeding — Water column
  • Propagation — Fragmentation; every piece grows on

Grower’s Notes

  • It has no roots and no rhizoids that grip properly. Unlike Java Moss it won't fasten itself to wood quickly — tuck it into crevices, tie it under mesh, or glue it, and give it months to settle.
  • It also works floating. A loose ball drifting at the surface is a legitimate way to keep it, and shrimp will graze it constantly either way.
  • Keep it out of strong flow. The fronds are light and unanchored, so a powerful outflow will simply relocate your Subwassertang to the far end of the tank.
  • It resists algae unusually well for a slow plant, which is why it holds up in long-term scapes where mosses eventually need stripping out.

products.title: Staurogyne Repens | Bulk Pack
products.body_html:
Carpeting a whole foreground one portion at a time is slow and expensive. Staurogyne repens spreads by creeping sideways rather than by runner, so the fastest route to a finished carpet is planting enough stems at the start — which is what this pack is for.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Staurogyne Repens cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, sold as loose fresh-cut stems in bulk pack sizes:

  • 10 Pack: Includes 10 portions, with approximately 6 loose fresh-cut stems per portion. Total approximately 60 stems.
  • 20 Pack: Includes 20 portions, with approximately 6 loose fresh-cut stems per portion. Total approximately 120 stems.
  • 30 Pack: Includes 30 portions, with approximately 6 loose fresh-cut stems per portion. Total approximately 180 stems.

Stems may arrive with some roots or without roots depending on growth stage and harvest condition. Each portion is freshly cut and prepared for planting in freshwater aquariums.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Staurogyne Repens, Creeping Staurogyne
  • Scientific name — Staurogyne repens
  • Origin — Rio Cristalino, Brazil
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Shipped size — 60 to 180 fresh-cut stems, roughly 2-4 in each
  • Mature height — 2-4 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium. More light means tighter, denser growth
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious creeping stem
  • Propagation — Cuttings — replant trimmed tops straight into the substrate

Grower's Notes

  • Buy enough to plant it properly. Staurogyne creeps rather than running, so it fills gaps slowly. Sixty stems planted two inches apart cover roughly a 12x12 inch area on day one — far faster than waiting for six stems to spread across it.
  • Plant the stems a couple of inches apart and let them creep together. Packed tight from day one, the inner stems shade each other and drop their lower leaves.
  • Trim the tops early rather than waiting for height. Every cut forces side shoots, and that branching is what turns a row of stems into an actual carpet.
  • Replant every trimming — cut tops root readily, so the carpet keeps expanding at no extra cost.
  • Yellowing lower leaves usually means light isn't reaching the base, either because the mat has thickened or a taller plant is shading it.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Staurogyne Repens Care Guide.

Notes

  • Pictures are not the actual plants you will receive, but a sample representation. Unless specified, we do not guarantee aquatic plants will be free of pests, snails, algae, or pesticides. Plants may be grown emersed or submerged. Some melting, leaf loss, or transition is normal as plants adapt to a new aquarium environment.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.body_html:
Theia runs warm — golden to copper-bronze with a soft iridescence, on narrow, gently curved leaves. It is one of the few Bucephalandra that reads gold rather than blue, green or red, which makes it useful where the rest of a scape is cool-toned.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Theia Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Theia'
  • Also known as — Buce Theia
  • Origin — Borneo (genus range)
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Very slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Stronger light lifts the gold and copper, but brings algae the plant is too slow to outgrow.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Speeds growth and enriches colour if you already run it.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed. Epiphyte; feeds from the water column.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rhizome creeper; grows submersed or emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Gold is the gap in most Buce collections. The genus runs heavily to blue, green, purple and red. A warm copper-gold sits against all of them, which is why Theia is worth having even if you already keep several varieties.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie or glue it to wood or rock and leave it exposed; buried rhizomes rot.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.
  • At under two inches of growth a year, coverage has to be bought rather than waited for. Start with more plants if you want a filled-in look.
  • Some leaf melt after shipping is normal. The rhizome survives and pushes new submersed leaves within a few weeks.

Not to be confused with Bucephalandra Theia Green, which is a separate variety.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Bucephalandra Care Guide.

Notes

Like most Bucephalandra, minor leaf melt may occur after introduction as the plant adjusts to new water parameters. This is normal and temporary — new submersed leaves regrow from the rhizome once the plant stabilizes.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Nymphaea Director George T. Moore | Violet-Purple Tropical Water Lily
products.body_html:
Nymphaea 'Director George T. Moore' is a stunning tropical water lily known for its captivating violet-purple flowers and robust growth. This aquatic plant is perfect for adding a splash of vibrant color to any pond or water garden.

Key Features:

  • Vibrant Violet-Purple Flowers: Boasts large, star-shaped flowers that are a striking violet-purple, adding a dramatic and elegant touch to your water garden. Each bloom measures 4-6 inches in diameter and is highly fragrant.
  • Lush Foliage: Features broad, rounded green leaves that provide a beautiful contrast to the vivid flowers, enhancing the overall aesthetic of your pond.
  • Prolific Blooming: Blooms profusely from June to frost, ensuring a long-lasting display of color throughout the growing season.

Optimal Conditions:

  • Sunlight: Thrives in full sun, requiring at least 6 hours of direct sunlight daily for optimal blooming.
  • Water Depth: Best planted at a depth of 12 to 24 inches in still or slow-moving water.
  • Soil Type: Prefers heavy clay or loam soils. Planting in containers submerged in the pond helps manage its growth and makes seasonal care easier.

Benefits:

  • Aesthetic Appeal: Enhances the visual appeal of any pond with its vibrant, showy flowers and lush foliage.
  • Wildlife Attraction: Attracts beneficial wildlife such as bees and dragonflies, contributing to a healthy pond ecosystem.
  • Fragrant Blooms: The flowers emit a pleasant fragrance, adding an extra sensory delight to your garden.

Care and Maintenance:

  • Fertilization: Regular fertilization during the growing season with aquatic plant fertilizer promotes healthy growth and abundant blooming.
  • Pruning: Remove yellowing leaves and spent flowers to encourage new growth and maintain plant health.
  • Winter Care: In cooler climates, treat this tropical lily as an annual or store the tubers in a cool, frost-free area until spring. This involves removing the tubers after the first frost, hosing them off, allowing them to dry for several days, and storing them in jars of distilled water or moist sand at temperatures around 50-55°F.

Conclusion:

Nymphaea 'Director George T. Moore' is a magnificent addition to any water garden, offering vibrant color, fragrant blooms, and a long blooming season. Its ease of care and stunning appearance make it a favorite among both novice and experienced gardeners. Add the captivating beauty of Nymphaea 'Director George T. Moore' to your pond today and enjoy the dynamic transformation it brings to your aquatic environment.

  • You will get 1 young and freshly harvested water lily tuber
  • All of our water lilies tubers/rhizomes have been inspected before ship out and guaranteed they are viable and perfect to grow in a proper pond environment

PLANTING INSTRUCTIONS FOR WATER LILY

 

There are two main types of water lilies, tropical and hardy. The differences between tropical and hardy water lilies are a growing habit. Tropical water lilies don't do well in winter. Hardy water lilies, on the other hand, can tolerate the cold. Tropical water lilies tubers must be removed from the pond and stored in moist conditions to come back in the future years. In warm climates, they can remain in the pond.

products.title: Hydrocotyle Tripartita Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Clover leaves, in a carpet. Hydrocotyle tripartita — widely sold as Hydrocotyle 'Japan' — spreads fast across the foreground in tight clusters of small three-lobed leaves. It is one of the quickest carpets to establish and one of the easiest to shape with scissors. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You’ll Receive

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Clover Plant, Hydrocotyle Japan
  • Scientific name — Hydrocotyle tripartita
  • Also known as — Hydrocotyle sp. 'Japan', Three-part Pennywort
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Light is what keeps it flat instead of climbing
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient substrate recommended
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Runners — cut and replant sections

Grower’s Notes

  • Light decides carpet or climber. Under strong light it hugs the substrate. Under weak light the runners stretch upward and it stops being a carpet — the single most common complaint about this plant, and it's a lighting problem, not a plant problem.
  • It grows fast enough to become a chore. Trim runners every few weeks or it crosses into neighbouring plants.
  • Pin fresh cuttings down with weights or tweezers until roots grab; loose sections float free.
  • Divide the tissue-culture portion into small clumps and plant them an inch apart rather than as one mass.
  • Compare with Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides — sturdier, thicker foliage, and quicker again.

Notes

  • Minor melting or yellowing may occur after planting while the plant adjusts to your tank conditions. With proper lighting and CO₂, new shoots and runners will appear rapidly.

products.title: Vallisneria spiralis 'Leopard'
products.body_html:
Want a background plant with markings rather than plain green? Vallisneria spiralis 'Leopard' carries dark spotting scattered along its ribbon leaves — the same easy, fast-spreading Val, with a pattern almost nothing else in a planted tank offers.

What You’ll Receive

  • Bunched plants | Approx. 2–3 plants bundled with foam and lead weight

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Leopard Vallisneria, also known as Spotted Val
  • Scientific name — Vallisneria spiralis 'Leopard'
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is widespread
  • Placement — Background, or back and side corners
  • Shipped size — Approx. 2-3 plants, roughly 5-10 in
  • Mature height — 10–20 in
  • Suits — 20 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. The spotting darkens under stronger light
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–8.0. Tolerates hard, alkaline water well
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic. Cannot be grown emersed
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • The spots need light to show. In a dim tank Leopard Val grows perfectly well but reads as ordinary green Vallisneria. If you bought it for the pattern, put it where light reaches.
  • Plant the crown at the substrate line, never below it. A buried crown rots — the usual reason a new Val fails in the first fortnight.
  • Feed at the roots. In inert gravel it survives but barely spreads; root tabs are what turn three plants into a stand.
  • Don't trim the tops to control height. Cut Val leaves brown at the cut and stay that way — remove whole leaves at the base instead.
  • Runners travel fast. Pull unwanted plantlets by hand rather than cutting, and expect to thin it every month or two once established.

products.body_html:

products.title: Aciotis Acuminifolia Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Colour on the underside, not the top. Aciotis acuminifolia grows deep green leaves backed with reddish-purple — so the plant reads green from above and flushes violet wherever a leaf turns or catches light from below. It is rare in the hobby, from tropical South America, and unrelated to anything else in a typical planted tank.

What You’ll Receive

Healthy, lab-grown Aciotis acuminifolia cultivated by Aquarium Plants Factory® in sterile Vitro Culture® conditions. Each 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag contains multiple healthy plantlets ready for planting and acclimation.

products.title: Flame Moss
products.body_html:
Every other moss sprawls sideways — Flame Moss grows up. Its fronds twist vertically in curling, flame-like columns, giving a planted tank a sense of movement and height that no other moss can produce.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a small loose portion, approx. 2" x 2" in size
  • Perfect to attached to driftwood, rock, or stone

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Flame Moss
  • Scientific name — Taxiphyllum sp. 'Flame'
  • Also sold as — Vesicularia sp. 'Flame'
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 2–4 in of upright growth
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light brings algae it grows too slowly to shed
  • CO₂ — Not required! Tighter and faster with it, perfectly happy without
  • Water — 70–82°F · pH 5.0–8.0, one of the widest ranges of any plant
  • Feeding — Water column
  • Propagation — Fragmentation; divide and reattach small sections

Grower’s Notes

  • Tie it in a thin, flat layer and let it rise on its own. The vertical growth is what you are paying for, and a thick clump smothers that shape before it forms.
  • Cooler water gives tighter flames. In warm tanks the fronds loosen and lengthen, losing the twisting column look.
  • Trim the tops rather than the sides. Cutting the tips forces new upright shoots and keeps the flame effect dense.
  • Be patient. It is slow even by moss standards and takes a couple of months to knit onto hardscape — that slowness is why it holds its shape so well.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference. Portion size, density and frond shape vary with temperature and growing conditions.

Grower's Notes

  • Plant it in a group, at the back. A single rosette of ribbon leaves is unremarkable. Several planted together where there is some flow give the swaying curtain effect that is the whole reason to choose a crispatula form over a broad-leaved crypt.
  • Give it substrate depth. Twelve to twenty inches of leaf needs a deep, well-fed root run. Two inches of nutrient substrate minimum, or root tabs pushed under each crown.

products.title: Hygrophila Difformis | Bulk Pack
products.body_html:
🌿 Hygrophila Difformis – Water Wisteria Bulk Pack | Fast-Growing Aquarium Stem Plant

Hygrophila difformis, commonly known as Water Wisteria, is one of the most popular and beginner-friendly aquarium plants in the hobby. This fast-growing aquatic stem plant is prized for its beautiful lace-like, fern-shaped leaves and vibrant green coloration that instantly adds lush density to planted aquariums.

Native to the Indian subcontinent, Water Wisteria is extremely adaptable and can thrive in a wide range of aquarium conditions. Its rapid growth helps absorb excess nutrients from the water column, making it an excellent natural ally for maintaining balanced and algae-controlled aquariums.

This Bulk Pack of Hygrophila Difformis is perfect for aquascapers, breeders, and planted tank enthusiasts who need large quantities of healthy stems to create dense backgrounds, jungle-style aquascapes, or nutrient-absorbing plant mass in aquariums.

🌟 Key Features

Scientific Name: Hygrophila difformis
Common Name: Water Wisteria
Plant Type: Freshwater stem plant

• Fast Growing: One of the fastest growing aquarium plants, ideal for stabilizing new tanks.
• Beautiful Leaf Structure: Features delicate, deeply lobed leaves that resemble aquatic ferns.
• Beginner Friendly: Extremely hardy and adaptable to various aquarium conditions.
• Excellent Nutrient Absorber: Helps reduce algae by consuming excess nutrients.

Propagation is extremely simple. Just trim the stems and replant the cuttings into the substrate. Each cutting will quickly develop new roots and continue growing.

Because of its rapid growth, Hygrophila difformis is commonly used in new aquariums to help establish biological balance and improve water quality.

  • Difficulty — Beginner

Grower's Notes

  • Buy coverage, do not wait for it. A single Anubias adds a few leaves a year. Twenty plants spread across a piece of wood look established the day they go in; one plant never will. That is the whole argument for buying in bulk.
  • Pointed leaves break up a wall of green. Massed Anubias can look like one undifferentiated clump. The spear shape of 'Peacock' gives a large planting internal texture without changing the care routine.
  • Space them further apart than looks right. Each rhizome needs water movement around it. Where rhizomes press together, detritus collects and rot starts.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Attach with cotton thread or a spot of gel glue; the roots grip the wood themselves within a couple of months.
  • The leathery leaves are usually left alone by fish, which makes a bulk Anubias planting one of the few that works in a goldfish or cichlid tank.

  • Origin — Cultivated hybrid; the genus is native to West and Central Africa

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Excess light means algae on slow-turning leaves.

Grower's Notes

  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots can go into substrate; the rhizome cannot. Buried, it rots — the most common way an Anubias is lost.
  • Buying in quantity is the only sensible way to cover a large piece of wood with a slow-growing plant. Anubias adds roughly one leaf every few weeks, so density has to come from the plants you start with, not from waiting.

  • Thick waxy leaves hold up in tanks that shred softer plants, which is why Anubias survives with cichlids and large fish where most planting fails.

products.title: Water Lettuce
products.body_html:
Want surface cover with real presence? Water Lettuce floats as soft velvety rosettes that genuinely look like small heads of lettuce, trailing long feathery roots beneath. It shades the water, strips nutrients, and gives fry and shrimp somewhere to hide.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as a small portion of loose, Lettuce rosettes (approximately 1–2 plants, depending on size and season).

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Water Lettuce
  • Scientific name — Pistia stratiotes
  • Placement — Floating
  • Mature size — 2–6 in across
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high. Full sun outdoors
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 70–85°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Calm surface, warm water
  • Substrate — Not required. Feeds entirely from the water column
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic, free floating
  • Propagation — Daughter plants on runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Keep the leaves dry. The velvety upper surface is not built to be wet — constant splash from a spray bar, strong HOB return or a dripping lid will rot the rosettes. Aim outflow below the surface, and leave an air gap under a closed lid.
  • The roots are the point. A dense trailing root curtain is where shrimplets and fry shelter, and where much of the nitrate uptake happens — resist trimming them for looks.
  • Thin it weekly. It multiplies fast by runner and a closed mat shades everything below.
  • It wants warmth and will not survive frost outdoors. In tropical and subtropical climates it spreads rapidly — monitor and maintain responsibly.

Want a smaller version for an aquarium? See Dwarf Water Lettuce, which stays 1–2 in across.

Want to go deeper? Read our guide to the Best Floating Plants for Freshwater Aquariums.

  • We will NOT ship Water Lettuce (Pistia stratiotes) to the following states or territories due to legal restrictions:
    Alabama (AL), California (CA), Florida (FL), Louisiana (LA), Mississippi (MS), South Carolina (SC), Texas (TX), Wisconsin (WI), Ohio (OH), Maine (ME), Puerto Rico (PR).

products.title: Dwarf Hairgrass
products.body_html:
Want a grass lawn underwater? Dwarf Hairgrass spreads by runner into a fine, meadow-like carpet — the classic foreground for Iwagumi and nature-style layouts, and the plant most people picture when they imagine a carpeted tank.

You may know it as Eleocharis parvula. That is the trade name — see the note below.

What You’ll Receive

  • Bare-root Plants | small clump portion, bare-root plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Dwarf Hairgrass
  • Scientific name — Eleocharis pusilla
  • Also known as — Eleocharis parvula (misapplied trade name)
  • Origin — Australia and New Zealand
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Shipped size — Small bare-root clump portion
  • Mature height — 3–6 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Why two scientific names?

Dwarf Hairgrass has been sold as Eleocharis parvula in the aquarium trade for a very long time, and most hobbyists still know it by that name.

Eleocharis parvula is a real species — but it is a brackish water plant, not suited to freshwater aquariums. Almost everything sold in the hobby under that label is in fact Eleocharis pusilla, a freshwater species.

So the plant you receive is Eleocharis pusilla: the same Dwarf Hairgrass you have always bought, correctly named, and genuinely suited to a freshwater tank.

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Light must reach the substrate for it to carpet rather than stretch
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Dry start works well
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Split the clump into many small portions. Divide into groups of a few blades and plant them an inch apart. Runners only travel into open substrate, so a single lump takes months longer to fill a foreground than the same plant spread out.
  • Keeping it alive is easy; carpeting it is not. That gap is why this is rated Intermediate. Survival needs little, but a dense low lawn needs strong light at substrate level and usually CO₂ — without both, expect a thin, stretched meadow.
  • Light reaching the substrate is what decides carpet versus stretch. Shaded hairgrass grows long and thin instead of dense and low.
  • Trim the carpet once established. Cutting it back encourages runner growth rather than height.
  • Expect the emersed blades to melt back after planting. New growth comes from the runners, not the original blades.

Want the shorter version? See Dwarf Hairgrass 'Mini', which stays 1–2 in.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Dwarf Hairgrass Care Guide.

products.body_html:
Want a plant that reacts when you touch it? Water Mimosa folds its delicate fern-like leaflets inward within seconds of being disturbed, then opens again once left alone. It floats on spongy buoyant stems, forming a soft green canopy — and it is the only plant we sell that moves on its own.

What You’ll Receive

Healthy Water Mimosa plants carefully prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®.

Variants available:

2 Plants – Unrooted
Fresh-cut floating plants without roots.

2 Plants – Rooted
Fresh-cut floating plants with visible developing roots.

10 Plants – Unrooted
Bulk portion of fresh-cut floating plants without roots.

10 Plants – Rooted
Bulk portion of fresh-cut floating plants with visible developing roots.

All plants are carefully selected and shipped fresh to ensure healthy arrival.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Water Mimosa, also known as Sensitive Water Mimosa
  • Scientific name — Neptunia oleracea
  • Placement — Floating
  • Mature height — 6–8 in above the surface
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 70–85°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Warmth matters more than most floaters
  • Substrate — Not required. Feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also roots in pond margins
  • Propagation — Plantlets along trailing stems

Grower’s Notes

  • The leaf movement is real and repeatable. Touch, vibration or a sudden change in light causes the leaflets to fold within a second or two, reopening over the next few minutes. It is the same mechanism as the terrestrial sensitive plant.
  • Keep the foliage dry. Like other floaters, the leaves sit above the waterline and rot if constantly splashed — aim filter outflow below the surface.
  • It wants warmth. Growth slows markedly at the cool end of its range, so this is a poor choice for an unheated tank.
  • Propagate by separating plantlets that form along the trailing stems and floating them on. It spreads quickly enough to need thinning.
  • Expect folded leaves on arrival. Transit stress makes it close up; it reopens within a day of being floated in stable conditions.

Want to go deeper? Read our guide to the Best Floating Plants for Freshwater Aquariums.

Notes

  • Aquatic plants may experience minor cosmetic changes during shipping due to temperature, handling, and transit time. Leaves may temporarily fold or show slight stress but typically recover quickly once placed in suitable aquarium or pond conditions.
  • Some aquatic plants are restricted in certain U.S. states — check before ordering, and never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.body_html:
Most Bucephalandra are bought for dark colour. Bucephalandra 'Green Wavy' is bought for shape — small, elongated leaves with a deep ruffle along the edge, in plain bright green. It clumps into miniature islands on wood and stone, and the wave gives texture where a dark Buce would just give shadow. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Green Wavy Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Green Wavy'
  • Also known as — Buce, Bucep
  • Origin — Riverbanks of Borneo

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium

  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed

Grower's Notes

  • Green Buce solves a problem dark Buce creates. On dark wood, a deep-red or blue Bucephalandra disappears. Green Wavy stays visible — same slow, undemanding plant, but it reads as texture rather than a shadow.

products.body_html:
Littorella uniflora looks like a fine grass carpet and behaves like nothing else in the hobby — it is a temperate plant from cool North American and European lake margins. Given water at the cooler end of the tropical range it forms a dense, low lawn by runner without ever growing tall.

What You'll Receive

  • Bag size: Approx. 4 inches. Yield 2-3 clump plants
  • Sustainable growth aquarium plants species

Plant Profile

  • Also known as — US Micro Sword, American Shore Grass, American Shoreweed
  • Origin — North America and northern Europe
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Mature height — 1-3 inches

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 65-75°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; this is a root feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower's Notes

  • Temperature is the deciding factor. This is a cool-water species. Held at 65-75°F it spreads steadily; run consistently warm, above the upper end, and it thins and stalls no matter what else is right. It suits an unheated or lightly heated tank far better than a tropical community.
  • Plant rosettes a few millimetres apart. Separate the culture into individual rosettes and set them close together. Each one throws runners outward, and tight initial spacing is what closes the carpet in months rather than a year.
  • Feed the substrate. Littorella is a root feeder with an unusually deep root system for its size. Aquasoil or root tabs under the planting area matter more than water column dosing.
  • Trim to keep it flat. Old leaves lengthen and lean over. Cutting the carpet back forces fresh short growth and stops the lower layer from being shaded out.
  • It is not Lilaeopsis. The two look nearly identical and are often confused, but they are unrelated plants from different families. Littorella prefers cooler water; care advice written for Lilaeopsis will not transfer cleanly.

products.title: Hygrophila Pink Chai Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Want neon pink rather than red? Hygrophila lancea 'Pink Chai' carries vivid pink through its stems and narrow elongated leaves — a colour no other stem plant in our range produces. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format, free of snails, algae and pesticide residue.

What You’ll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing multiple Hygrophila Pink Chai plantlets, ready for rinsing, acclimation, and planting.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pink Chai
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila lancea 'Pink Chai'
  • Also known as — Hygrophila sp. 'Pink Chai', Hygrophila sp. 'Chai', Hygrophila Pink Lady
  • Origin — Natural hybrid of Hygrophila lancea 'Araguaia', found at South Island Aquarium in Singapore
  • Placement — Midground
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 in
  • Mature height — 4–10 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium. Stronger light intensifies the pink
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5. Sensitive to sudden changes
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Stability matters more than intensity. Pink Chai reacts to sudden shifts in parameters more than most Hygrophila. A steady tank produces better colour than a heavily dosed one that swings.
  • Occasional stems revert. The hybrid is stable and cuttings normally come true pink, but a stem may sometimes return to the reddish-brown of the parent Hygrophila lancea 'Araguaia'. That is the hybrid behaving normally, not a mislabelled plant — remove reverted stems if you want the stand to stay uniformly pink.
  • Divide the cup into small clumps and plant them a little apart. Tissue culture stock establishes faster with space around it.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before planting or it clouds water and feeds algae in the first weeks.
  • Trim regularly and replant the tops. Topping forces branching, which is what turns a few stems into a block of colour.

Prefer rooted plants? See Hygrophila Pink Chai (Small Size) or the standard size.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Hygrophila Chai Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are sample representations. Actual colouration may vary depending on light intensity, CO₂, and nutrients. Growth form may differ during emersed-to-submerged transition.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Anubias Broad White Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Anubias Broad White carries some of the heaviest white variegation of any Anubias — wide leaves marbled cream and green, with individual leaves sometimes coming through almost entirely white. This is the tissue-culture format, which is the cheapest way into a plant that is otherwise expensive per rhizome.

What You'll Receive

Fresh, healthy Anubias Broad White cultivated using Vitro Culture® tissue culture technology and sealed in sterile media for optimal quality and transport.

Pack Options Available:

1 Bag: One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing healthy Anubias Broad White plantlets.
5 Bags: Five 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bags containing healthy Anubias Broad White plantlets.
10 Bags: Ten 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bags containing healthy Anubias Broad White plantlets.

Each bag contains multiple young plantlets ready to rinse, separate, acclimate, and plant in your aquarium or high-humidity emersed setup.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Broad White Anubias
  • Scientific name — Anubias barteri 'Broad White'
  • Origin — Cultivated variety; the genus is native to West and Central Africa
  • Placement — Midground, attached to wood or stone
  • Mature height — 6-10 inches
  • Growth rate — Very slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light is the fastest way to lose this plant — see the note below.
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • White tissue has no chlorophyll, which is what makes this an advanced plant. A heavily variegated leaf produces far less energy than a green one, so growth is slower, damage takes longer to recover from, and algae gets a head start on the white areas. Keep it shaded and it will be fine; put it under a strong light and it will decline.
  • Rinse the gel off and separate the plantlets before mounting. Attach the rhizome to wood or stone — never bury it.
  • Tissue-culture plants start very small, and a very slow plant with reduced chlorophyll starts slower still. Give this one a season before judging it.
  • Variegation is unpredictable. Some leaves come mostly white, some mostly green. An all-white leaf will eventually exhaust itself and drop — that is normal, not a fault.
  • Sterile media means no snails, algae or pesticide residue, which is why this format suits shrimp tanks.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Anubias Care Guide.

Notes

Plants grown in tissue culture are produced in sterile laboratory environments and may appear smaller than mature aquarium plants. Once introduced into the aquarium with proper lighting and nutrients, they will gradually adapt and develop into fully established plants.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Echinodorus Pink Princess Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
A sword plant in pastel. Echinodorus 'Pink Princess' — also sold as Pink Amazon Sword — grows smooth lanceolate leaves in blush pink to soft rose rather than the usual green or burgundy, on a tidy upright rosette. This is the sterile tissue culture version.

What You'll Receive

  • Vitro Culture® Bag (4-inch): You will receive one sealed 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag containing approximately 4 small Pink Princess Sword plantlets, cultivated in a sterile lab environment. Simply rinse the nutrient gel under clean water, gently separate the plantlets, and plant them in your substrate.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pink Princess Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus 'Pink Princess'
  • Also known as — Pink Amazon Sword
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the genus is native to the Americas
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10-16 inches
  • Suits — 20 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — aquasoil or root tabs under the crown.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette; also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on aerial floral stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Plantlets arrive light green. Pink develops as the leaves mature under your own lighting, usually over the first month or two. A bag that looks plain green on day one is normal, not mislabelled.
  • Root tabs are what hold the pink. Swords feed almost entirely through their roots. Without a fertilised root zone the colour washes out and growth slows, no matter how bright the light is.
  • Never bury the crown. Cover the roots and leave the growing point at substrate level. A buried crown rots from the centre and does not recover.
  • Separate the plantlets before planting. Rinse the gel off and plant the four individually with space between them. Planted as a clump they shade each other and the inner ones fail.
  • Light intensity decides the shade of pink. Medium light gives a pale blush; stronger light deepens it toward rose. It is the one variable worth adjusting if the colour disappoints.

Two ways to buy this plant. This listing is the 4-inch Vitro Culture® bag — about four sterile plantlets, the cheapest way in and roughly a year of growing on. There is also an established plant, bare-root, bunched or potted, if you want colour this season.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Amazon Sword & Echinodorus Care Guide.

Notes

  • Coloration may vary based on lighting intensity, nutrients, and tank conditions. Younger plantlets may appear light green and gradually develop pink tones as they mature. Avoid burying the crown during planting.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Cuphea Anagalloidea
products.body_html:
Cuphea anagalloidea is a delicate small stem plant that requires a lot of care.
The brilliant shade of scarlet that may be found on the upper surface of the submerged leaves is brought out to its fullest potential when exposed to bright light. This plant was initially introduced into the aquarium hobby under the name Rotala sp. Araguaia; however, it was later determined that it belongs to the Cuphea species. Cuphea Anagalloidea can only grow vertically. It looks best when used in a group in the middleground as a color accent. The upper edges of the leaves turn a bright crimson to orange-red color under high lighting, but the stem remains green. Sufficient lighting, with plenty CO2 and nutrients, and soft water are all recommended.
