products.title: Bucephalandra Giant Velvet
products.body_html:
Matte, not glossy. Bucephalandra sp. 'Giant Velvet' has a soft velvet surface on broad dark green leaves — it absorbs light where most Buce reflect it, giving depth rather than shine. "Giant" is relative: at 4–6 inches it is large for a Bucephalandra, where most of the genus sits at 2–3.

products.body_html:

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner

Grower's Notes

  • Expect roughly an inch of growth per year. Buce is among the slowest plants sold. Most arrive around 2-3 inches and stay close to that for a long time, which is exactly why it holds a scape's composition without trimming.
  • Never bury the rhizome. The horizontal stem must sit in open water, tied or glued to a surface. Buried, it rots — and at this growth rate the loss is not recoverable in a season.

products.title: Ceratopteris Siliquosa
products.body_html:
Want a fast plant that propagates itself? Water Sprite grows fine, lacy fern foliage that fills a background in weeks — planted or floating, your choice — and produces new plants along its own leaf margins with no effort from you.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as Fresh-cut Plants, Bunched Plants or Potted Plants:

  • Fresh-cut Plants: Approximately 6 loose fresh-cut plants without root.
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 6 fresh-cut plants without root bundled with a plant weight for easy placement.
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 6 fresh-cut plants without root potted in rockwool and a net pot for secure growth and easy placement.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Water Sprite, Narrow Leaf Water Sprite
  • Scientific name — Ceratopteris thalictroides 'Siliquosa'
  • Placement — Midground to background, or floating
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Feeds mainly from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Plantlets on leaf margins

Grower’s Notes

  • It clones itself along its leaves. Small plantlets form on the leaf edges and on older leaves as they age. Once one has a few fronds and roots, detach it and plant or float it — this is how a single portion becomes a tankful without you doing anything.
  • Planted or floating are both correct. Floating it grows faster and shades the tank below; planted it grows more upright. Floating is the usual choice in fry and shrimp tanks.
  • It strips nitrate quickly, which makes it genuinely useful in a new or heavily stocked tank rather than just decorative.
  • Roots are fragile when planted. Bury only enough to hold it and let it anchor itself, or it tears loose.

Water Sprite is not Water Wisteria. This is a true fern, growing as a rosette and reproducing from leaf plantlets. Water Wisteria is Hygrophila difformis — a flowering stem plant with paired leaves up an upright stem. Both have finely divided foliage, which is where the confusion starts.

products.title: Ludwigia Meta
products.body_html:
Ludwigia Meta is what people reach for when Ludwigia Pantanal has beaten them. It gives the same fine whorls of narrow leaves and the same orange-to-red burn under strong light, but without Pantanal's intolerance for anything less than perfect. Still uncommon in the trade, and still a centrepiece plant.

What You'll Receive

Choose the format that suits your aquascaping needs:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 6+ unrooted stems
  • Bunched Plants: 6+ fresh-cut stems without root, bundled with foam and plant weight
  • Potted Plants: 6+ fresh-cut stems potted in rockwool within a 2-inch net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ludwigia Meta
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia inclinata var. verticillata 'Meta'
  • Also known as — Ludwigia sp. 'Meta'
  • Origin — Departamento del Meta, central Colombia
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 6-14 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.0. Soft water, carbonate hardness below 4°dH
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs, plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • It arrives green and it is supposed to. Our stock is grown emersed, where the leaves are plain green. Orange and red develop only after the plant converts to submersed growth under your lighting — usually three to four weeks in.
  • Soft water matters more than light. Meta colours and grows best with carbonate hardness under 4°dH. In hard water it stays green and slowly stalls no matter how much light and iron you throw at it — test KH rather than chasing a pH number.
  • Easier than Pantanal, same look. If you have lost Ludwigia Pantanal to melt or stunting, Meta gives a similar fine-leaved red without the same intolerance of imperfect conditions.
  • It branches poorly, so plant more stems. Meta grows straight up with little side-shooting. Density comes from planting a group close together, not from waiting for one stem to bush out.
  • Replant the tops, discard the bases. As with most fine-leaved Ludwigia, the lower stem goes bare with age. Cut the top few inches, replant them, and pull the old base.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Ludwigia Care Guide.

Notes

  • Ludwigia Meta ships in its emersed green form. Once submerged and provided with strong light and nutrients, it will gradually develop its iconic orange to red hues. Slight leaf melt during transition is normal.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Ludwigia sp. White
products.body_html:
Want white foliage rather than red? Ludwigia inclinata var. verticillata 'White' produces slender leaves in pale pink through near-white — a colour almost nothing else in a planted tank offers. It is also one of the most demanding stem plants we sell, and worth understanding before you buy.

  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Central and South America

  • Mature height — 6–14 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High. Non-negotiable for the white and pink colouring
  • CO₂ — Required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient soil, root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Leaf form changes completely between emersed and submersed

Grower’s Notes

  • The pale colour is why it is difficult. White and pale pink tissue carries very little chlorophyll, so the plant photosynthesises inefficiently and has far less margin than a green or even a red Ludwigia. High light and stable CO₂ are not optional extras here — they are what keep it alive.
  • Stability matters more than any single value. It reacts badly to swinging CO₂ or a large water change, and typically responds by melting from the lower stem upward.
  • Handle it by the base only. The fine whorled leaves strip where you grip, and bare nodes do not refoliate.
  • Trim and replant the tops. Lower sections rarely recover well enough to be worth keeping on a plant this slow to build.
  • It arrives green or greenish. The pink and white develop only once it has converted to submersed growth under strong light — judge the colour after a few weeks.

products.body_html:

  • Origin — Tropical Asia and Africa

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner

  • Trimming is what keeps it short. Left alone this species climbs well past a foot and eventually uproots itself under its own weight. Cut it back regularly and it holds the 2-6 inch height that makes it useful at the front of a tank.

products.body_html:
Aragon is one of the compact Bucephalandra varieties — small dark leaves on a tight rhizome, slow enough that a single piece holds its shape on a rock for years. Like every Buce it wants attaching rather than planting, and very little else.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Aragon Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Aragon'
  • Also known as — Buce, Bucep; tribe Schismatoglottideae, family Araceae
  • Origin — Borneo, Indonesia
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to hardscape

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed; tie or glue the rhizome to wood or rock
  • Growth habit — Amphibious epiphyte, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Expect roughly an inch of growth per year. Bucephalandra is among the slowest plants sold. Most arrive around 2-3 inches and stay close to that for a long time — which is exactly why it holds a scape's composition without trimming.
  • Never bury the rhizome. The horizontal stem must sit in open water, tied or glued to a surface. Buried, it rots, and a plant this slow does not grow back from that in a season.

  • It suits a nano tank. At two to four inches, Aragon works in a shrimp tank or small scape where a larger Buce would dominate.

products.title: Echinodorus Aflame Vitro Culture (Purple Knight Sword)
products.body_html:
Echinodorus 'Aflame' is a sword plant that skips the green stage. New leaves emerge burgundy and darken toward purple-black as they harden, held in an upright rosette rather than the sprawling form most swords take. It gives a planted tank a red centrepiece without a single stem plant.

What You'll Receive

  • You will receive one sealed 4-inch Vitro Culture bag containing approximately 3–4 young Echinodorus Aflame plantlets

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Purple Knight Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus 'Aflame'
  • Also known as — Aflame Sword
  • Origin — Cultivated hybrid; parent species from South America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10-16 inches

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; this is a root feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on flower stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Root tabs are what produce the colour. Swords take nearly all their nutrition from the substrate. Water column dosing alone gives you a pale, slow Aflame; a fertilised root zone gives you the burgundy the plant is bought for.
  • Never bury the crown. The growing point at the centre of the rosette must sit at substrate level. Covered, it rots — the leaves go first and the plant does not come back.
  • Plantlets arrive green. Tissue culture stock is grown under conditions that favour growth over pigment. Red and purple develop as the plant establishes under your lighting, usually over the first month or two.
  • It propagates from flower stalks, not runners. A mature Aflame sends up an inflorescence that produces daughter plants along its length. Let each grow roots and two or three leaves before cutting it free.
  • Old outer leaves are meant to be removed. Swords continuously shed their oldest leaves as new ones emerge from the centre. Cutting yellowing outer leaves at the base keeps the rosette tidy and stops them fouling the water.

  • Two different plants share the name "Giant Hairgrass." This one spreads by runners into a connected meadow. Eleocharis vivipara does not — it makes plantlets on its leaf tips instead. If you want a spreading stand, this is the one.
  • Split the portion into small tufts and plant them an inch apart. Runners close the gaps far faster than one dense clump would.
  • Feed at the roots — runner production stalls without a nutrient substrate or root tabs.
  • Trim the blades to control height; cutting doesn't harm the plant and encourages new runners.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before planting or it clouds water and feeds algae early on. Tissue culture arrives free of snails, algae and pesticide.

Notes

  • Vitro Culture® plants must be rinsed thoroughly to remove gel before planting. Minor melting or adjustment may occur as the plant transitions to submerged conditions. This is normal under proper care.

products.title: Utricularia Graminifolia
products.body_html:
A carnivorous plant that carpets. Utricularia graminifolia — UG — forms a fine, fluffy lawn of bright green grass-like leaves under an inch tall. It's a bladderwort: microscopic traps on its stolons catch protozoa. Fish and shrimp are in no danger whatsoever, and the carpet it makes is one of the finest-textured in the hobby.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a small loose bare-root portion
  • Approx. 2" x 2" in size

Plant Profile

  • Common name — UG, Grass-leaved Bladderwort
  • Scientific name — Utricularia graminifolia
  • Placement — Foreground carpet
  • Mature height — 0.5–1 in
  • Growth rate — Fast, once established

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High
  • CO₂ — Required
  • Water — 68–78°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Prefers soft, acidic water and cooler temperatures
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich soil
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Stolons

Grower’s Notes

  • Pin it down or lose it. UG has almost no root system when it arrives — it floats away at the first water change. Use stainless steel pins or small stones to hold the mat flat until it anchors, usually two to three weeks.
  • The dry start method transforms it. Planted in damp substrate under a covered tank with no standing water, UG has unlimited access to atmospheric CO₂ and carpets far faster than it will submerged. Flood the tank once the carpet has closed.
  • It is carnivorous but harmless — the traps are microscopic and target protozoa, not shrimp or fry.
  • Once anchored it develops a deep interconnected root mat, which is why an established UG carpet is remarkably stable.
  • Soft acidic water suits it. In hard alkaline tap water it struggles regardless of light.

products.title: Echinodorus Aflame (Purple Knight Sword)
products.body_html:
Echinodorus 'Aflame' is a sword plant that skips the green stage. New leaves emerge burgundy and darken toward purple as they harden, held in an upright rosette rather than the sprawling form most swords take. It gives a planted tank a red centrepiece without a single stem plant.

What You'll Receive

Enhance your aquarium with our versatile selection of high-quality aquatic plants, available in three convenient formats:

  • Bare-root Plants: Includes approximately 1 rooted plant without any potting material – perfect for flexible planting and customization.
  • Rooted Bunched: Includes approximately 1 rooted plant, bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement upon arrival.
  • Rooted Potted: Includes approximately 1 rooted plant securely potted in rockwool and a net pot, offering stability and healthy growth right out of the box.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Purple Knight Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus 'Aflame'
  • Also known as — Aflame Sword
  • Origin — Cultivated hybrid; parent species from South America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs; this is a root feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on flower stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Root tabs are what produce the colour. Swords take nearly all their nutrition from the substrate. Water column dosing alone gives you a pale, slow Aflame; a fertilised root zone gives you the burgundy the plant is bought for.
  • Never bury the crown. The growing point at the centre of the rosette must sit at substrate level. Covered, it rots — the leaves go first and the plant does not come back.
  • Emersed-grown stock resets after planting. The leaves it arrives with were formed out of water and will often melt away. Judge the plant on the leaves that follow, not the ones it came with.
  • It propagates from flower stalks, not runners. A mature Aflame sends up an inflorescence that produces daughter plants along its length. Let each grow roots and two or three leaves before cutting it free.
  • Old outer leaves are meant to be removed. Swords continuously shed their oldest leaves as new ones emerge from the centre. Cutting yellowing outer leaves at the base keeps the rosette tidy and stops them fouling the water.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Amazon Sword & Echinodorus Care Guide.

Notes

  • Coloration may vary depending on lighting, nutrient availability, and tank conditions. For best results, provide enriched root tabs and CO₂. Avoid burying the crown of the plant to prevent rot.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.body_html:

    You will receive five (5) individual 4-inch Vitro Culture® bags, each yielding approximately 3–4 healthy clump plants.

Each bag is grown in sterile Vitro Culture® conditions and is free from algae, snails, and pests. Plantlets are ready to rinse, divide, and plant directly into nutrient-rich substrate.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Micro Sword, also known as Brazilian Micro Sword
  • Scientific name — Lilaeopsis brasiliensis
  • Origin — South America
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Mature height — 1–3 in
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Light reaching the substrate is what makes it carpet
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required. It carpets faster and denser with it
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Fine, nutrient-rich substrate — root feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Divide the cup into many small clumps. Plant them an inch apart and let the runners close the gaps. Planted as one mass it takes months longer, because runners only travel into open substrate.
  • Root tabs decide the outcome. In inert gravel Micro Sword survives but never thickens — the most common reason a carpet stalls.
  • Use fine substrate. Its roots are short and delicate and cannot grip coarse gravel, so clumps float free before they anchor.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before planting or it clouds water and feeds algae in the first weeks.
  • It is slow to start. Expect little visible progress for the first month while it roots, then steady spread.

Despite the name, this is not a sword plant. Lilaeopsis is unrelated to Echinodorus (Amazon Swords) or Helanthium (chain swords) — it stays small and carpets, where true swords grow large or spread as rosettes.

products.title: Golden Nesaea
products.body_html:
Yellow is the rarest colour in a planted tank. Golden Nesaea (Ammannia pedicellata 'Golden') grows luminous golden-yellow foliage — not a pale green, not an orange-red, but a genuine gold that reads as a light source among green and red neighbours. Almost nothing else in the hobby does this.

  • Also known as — Ammannia pedicellata 'Golden'
  • Origin — Tanzania and Mozambique

  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Background

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner

  • The colour sits on the top leaves. Cherry pink develops on new growth nearest the light; lower leaves stay green. Trimming and replanting the tops is what keeps a stand looking red rather than green with a red fringe.
  • Iron, not light alone. Under medium light with steady micronutrient dosing the tops flush cherry. Strong light without iron gives you a fast green Hygrophila instead.
  • It is fast, so plan on trimming. Ten to twenty inches arrives quickly. Topping the stems and replanting the cuttings keeps the group at the height you want and doubles your plant count each time.
  • Beginner difficulty is genuine here. Unlike most red plants this is a hardy Hygrophila underneath. It will grow in a low-tech tank — you simply get less colour without dosing.
  • Plant the stems apart. Bunched stems rot where the foam and weight sit. Separate them and space each half an inch apart so light reaches the lower nodes.

products.title: Hyptis Lorentziana (Purple Mint)
products.body_html:
Hyptis lorentziana is an aquarium mint. Deep purple-red leaves in opposite pairs on square stems, from a genus better known for culinary herbs than for aquascapes — and still uncommon enough that most people have never seen it in a tank.

What You'll Receive

Enhance your aquarium with our versatile selection of high-quality aquatic plants, available in three convenient formats:

  • Fresh-Cut Bunched: Approximately 3+ fresh-cut stems without roots, bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement.

Choose the format that best suits your aquascaping needs and create a vibrant, lush underwater environment with our premium aquatic plants.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Purple Mint
  • Scientific name — Hyptis lorentziana
  • Also known as — formerly circulated as "Hemigraphis traian"
  • Family — Lamiaceae, the mint family
  • Origin — South America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 6-14 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-78°F, pH 6.0-7.0
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs, plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • It was misidentified for years. The plant circulated in the hobby as "Hemigraphis traian" until 2009, when it was correctly placed in Hyptis, in the mint family. Old care advice written under the wrong name is still floating around — worth knowing if you search for it.
  • Cut above a leaf pair, not mid-stem. Trim roughly three to four inches above the substrate, directly above a pair of leaves. That is what triggers the lateral shoots that turn one stem into a bush.
  • Strong light holds the purple. Under medium light it leans green-bronze. The deep purple-red the plant is bought for needs intensity plus consistent iron dosing.
  • It gets big in the wild and stays manageable in a tank. Emersed at a pond margin it reaches two metres; submersed and trimmed it stays in the 6-14 inch range.
  • Plant stems individually. Square-stemmed plants rot readily where a bunching band sits. Separate them and space each half an inch apart.

products.title: Vallisneria nana 'Striped'
products.body_html:
Want pattern on a narrow-leaved Val? Vallisneria nana 'Striped' — also sold as Tiger Val — carries brown striping and speckling along slim green blades. It gives you markings and movement without the solid curtain a broad-leaved Vallisneria creates.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as loose bare-root plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Bare-root Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual loose, bare-root plants
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Striped Vallisneria Nana, also known as Tiger Vallisneria
  • Scientific name — Vallisneria nana 'Striped'
  • Also known as — Vallisneria nana 'Tiger'
  • Placement — Background
  • Mature height — 20–30 in
  • Leaf width — Narrow, though noticeably wider than standard nana
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–8.0. Tolerates hard, alkaline water well
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • It stays green under strong light. This is the practical difference from Vallisneria spiralis 'Leopard', which develops red tones and heavier marbling under intensity. Striped keeps its green base with brown tiger markings whatever you throw at it.
  • Striping varies plant to plant, and some leaves carry more than others. That is normal for this cultivar rather than a sign of a poor specimen.
  • Plant the crown at the substrate line, never below it. A buried crown rots — the usual reason a new Val fails in the first fortnight.
  • Feed at the roots. In inert gravel it survives but barely spreads; root tabs are what turn three plants into a stand.
  • Don't trim the tops to control height. Cut Val leaves brown at the cut and stay that way — remove whole leaves at the base instead.

Want the finest blade instead? Standard Vallisneria nana is the narrowest in the genus at roughly 1 mm, without the markings.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Vallisneria Care Guide.

Notes

  • Some leaf melting may occur when transitioning to a new tank. Stripe intensity and patterning may vary between individual plants. Provide stable lighting and substrate for best performance.

products.title: Hygrophila Corymbosa
products.body_html:
Big leaves, fast. Hygrophila corymbosa — Giant Hygro or Temple Plant — grows broad, bright green leaves on sturdy upright stems and reaches 10–20 inches quickly without CO₂. Where fine-leaved stems give texture, this gives mass, which is exactly what a bare background needs.

  • Fresh-cut Potted | approx. 5 fresh-cut plants potted with net pot and rock wool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Corymbosa, Giant Hygro, Temple Plant
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila corymbosa
  • Also known as — Nomaphila corymbosa, Hygrophila stricta
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 5 fresh-cut stems, roughly 4-8 in
  • Mature height — 10–20 in

Care

  • Substrate — Nutrient substrate or root tabs recommended

Grower’s Notes

  • Leaf size is the reason to choose it. Most fast background stems are fine-leaved. Corymbosa's broad leaves read as solid green from a distance, which is why Dutch-style layouts use it to build depth against narrow-leaved neighbours.

products.title: Hygrophila Kompakt
products.body_html:
Want a Hygrophila that stays in the midground? Hygrophila corymbosa 'Kompakt' is the dwarf cultivar — broad bright green oval leaves on stems with much shorter internodes, so it grows into a dense low bush instead of running for the surface like standard corymbosa.

  • Fresh-Cut Potted: About 3+ fresh-cut stems without roots, securely potted in a net pot with rockwool, ensuring stability and healthy growth.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Kompakt, also known as Compact Hygrophila
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila corymbosa 'Kompakt'
  • Also known as — Nomaphila siamensis 'Parvifolia'
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Midground
  • Shipped size — Approx. 3+ fresh-cut stems, roughly 3-6 in
  • Mature height — 4–8 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium. Stronger light keeps the internodes short and the bush tight
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed in paludariums
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops and side shoots

Grower’s Notes

  • Short internodes are the whole point. Standard Hygrophila corymbosa stretches to 20 inches and beyond with wide gaps between leaf pairs. 'Kompakt' packs them close, which is why it holds a hedge shape where the parent plant does not — and why it fits a 10-gallon tank that the parent would swamp.
  • Light keeps it compact. Under weak light the internodes lengthen and it loses the dwarf habit — trimming won't bring it back.
  • Trim and replant the tops. Each cut forces side shoots, which is how a few stems become a solid midground block.
  • Root tabs help noticeably. It draws from both roots and water column, and leaf size drops in inert gravel.
  • Also available as sterile Kompakt Vitro Culture.

products.title: Cameroon Moss
products.body_html:
Leaves big enough to see. Cameroon Moss from West Africa grows overlapping rounded leaves along creeping stems, forming a dense cushion rather than a fine haze — which is why it also travels under the name Giant Pearl Moss. Attach it to wood or stone and it builds a thick green mat.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a small portion, loose moss
  • Approx. 2" x 2" / 5cm x 5cm portion

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Cameroon Moss
  • Scientific name — Vesicularia sp. 'Cameroon'
  • Also known as — Giant Pearl Moss, Plagiochilaceae sp. Cameroon
  • Origin — Cameroon, West Africa
  • Placement — Midground, attached to driftwood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 2–4 in

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Strong light brings algae into the cushion
  • CO₂ — Not required

  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed

Grower’s Notes

  • Leaf size is what you're buying. Java and Christmas Moss read as texture; Cameroon's larger overlapping leaves stay legible up close, which makes it worth placing at the front where it will actually be seen.
  • Tie it thinly and let it thicken. A dense pad traps detritus and rots from underneath.
  • It absorbs nutrients straight from the water column, so liquid dosing does more here than anything in the substrate.
  • Slow growth means it holds a shape for months — but also that algae, once in it, is very hard to clear.
  • It works well as a spawning surface for egg-scattering fish and as shrimp grazing ground.

products.title: Mini Christmas Moss
products.body_html:
Want the Christmas Moss shape at nano scale? Mini Christmas Moss branches into the same triangular fir-tree fronds as the standard form, at roughly half the size — which means the pattern stays visible on small hardscape instead of reading as a green blur.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as small, loose portion
  • Approx. 2 inches in size

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mini Christmas Moss, also known as Mini Xmas Moss
  • Scientific name — Vesicularia montagnei 'Mini'
  • Also known as — Taxiphyllum sp. 'Mini Christmas', Vesicularia sp. 'Mini Christmas'
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 1–2 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. High light grows algae, not moss
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5. Cooler water gives tighter branching
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape

  • Cooler water keeps the shape. Like standard Christmas Moss, the tight triangular branching is a cool-water trait. In a warm tank it grows looser and longer and starts to look like ordinary Java Moss — the small size makes that loss more obvious, not less.

  • Trim regularly. Each cut forces branching, which is what keeps the fir-tree structure crisp rather than stringy.
  • Never bury it in substrate, and never let algae establish — there is no safe way to remove algae from moss.

products.title: Bucephalandra Round Wavy
products.body_html:
Round Wavy pairs a short, rounded leaf with a rippled margin — a denser, more compact look than the elongated Bucephalandra varieties. It stays small enough for nano hardscape and never needs trimming.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a Bunched Plants or Potted Plants.
  • Pictures are not the actual plants you will receive, but a sample representation.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Round Wavy Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Round Wavy'
  • Also known as — Buce, Bucep
  • Origin — Borneo (genus range)
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5

  • Growth habit — Amphibious rhizome creeper; grows submersed or emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • Round leaves read as texture, not shape. On a small mount the individual leaf disappears and what you see is a dense green cushion — which is why this variety works better as ground cover on stone than as a specimen plant.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie or glue it to wood or rock and leave it exposed; buried rhizomes rot.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.
  • Some leaf melt after shipping is normal. The rhizome survives and pushes new submersed leaves within a few weeks.
  • Moderate flow keeps debris off the leaves. In dead water, slow-growing Buce collects detritus and then algae.

Minor leaf melt may occur after introduction as the plant adjusts to new water parameters. This is normal and temporary — new submersed leaves regrow from the rhizome once the plant stabilizes.

products.title: Bucephalandra Giant Broad Leaf
products.body_html:
Bucephalandra is a small-leaved genus. 'Giant Broad Leaf' is the exception — wide, thick, paddle-shaped leaves in deep green with a blue-metallic sheen under the right light. It is still a Buce, so it still grows about an inch a year; you are buying leaf size, not speed.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose bare-root plants:

  • 1 Plant: Loose bare-root with approximately 6+ leaves
  • 5 Plants: Loose bare-root with approximately 25+ leaves total
  • 10 Plants: Loose bare-root with approximately 50+ leaves total

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Giant Broad Leaf Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Giant Broad Leaf'
  • Also known as — Buce Giant Broad Leaf
  • Origin — Borneo, Indonesia
  • Placement — Midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 4-6 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required, though it speeds an already slow plant
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed; tie or glue the rhizome to wood or rock
  • Growth habit — Amphibious epiphyte, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • "Giant" means 4 to 6 inches, not enormous. Among Bucephalandra that is genuinely large — most varieties ship around 2-3 inches — but set expectations against the genus, not against a sword plant.
  • Expect roughly an inch of growth per year. Broad leaves do not mean fast growth. The plant you receive is close to the plant you will have in six months, which is exactly why it holds a scape's shape without trimming.
  • Never bury the rhizome. The horizontal stem must sit in open water, tied or glued to a surface. Buried, it rots — and at this growth rate the loss is not recoverable in a season.
  • The blue sheen needs an angle. Metallic iridescence on Buce shows when light strikes the leaf sideways. Mounted flat and viewed from above it simply reads dark green — position it on the side of wood or rock instead.
  • Melt after shipping is normal. Leaves may drop in the first fortnight while the rhizome settles. Leave it attached and undisturbed; new growth comes from the rhizome, not the old leaves.

Notes

  • Like most Bucephalandra, slight leaf melt may occur after introduction as the plant adjusts to new conditions. This is temporary—new submersed leaves will regrow from the rhizome once the plant stabilizes.

products.title: Hygrophila Odora
products.body_html:
🌿 Hygrophila Odora – Narrow-Leaf Green Alternative to Water Wisteria & Hygrophila pinnatifida

Hygrophila odora is a rare and visually striking African stem plant that combines the delicate, finely divided look of  Water Wisteria (Hygrophila difformis) with the bold, architectural appeal of Hygrophila pinnatifida—while maintaining a clean, vibrant green coloration.

The leaf shape closely resembles Water Wisteria but is much narrower and more refined, giving the plant a sharper, more structured appearance. At the same time, its overall form and texture are very similar to Hygrophila pinnatifida, making Hygrophila odora an excellent green alternative for aquascapers who love pinnatifida’s look but prefer to avoid brown or reddish tones.

When grown submersed, Hygrophila odora produces elegant, deeply lobed green leaves on upright stems, making it ideal for midground to background placement. In emersed form, the leaves broaden slightly, develop a soft texture, and release a natural aromatic scent when touched—a rare and unique trait among aquarium plants.

  • Scientific Name: Hygrophila odora
  • Common Name: Hygrophila Afrika
  • Origin: West Africa
  • Growth Rate: Medium
  • Placement: Midground to Background
  • Color: Bright to deep green
  • Leaf Shape: Narrow, finely divided (similar to Water Wisteria, but slimmer)
  • Comparable To: Hygrophila difformis (Water Wisteria), Hygrophila pinnatifida
  • Unique Trait: Aromatic foliage when grown emersed
  • Difficulty: Beginner to Advanced

🌱 Growth & Propagation

  • CO₂: Recommended for best structure and faster growth
  • Growth Method: Stem plant
  • Nutrient Substrate: Required
  • Can Be Grown Emersed: Yes
  • Propagation: Trim and replant healthy stem cuttings

With adequate nutrients and CO₂, Hygrophila odora grows strong, upright stems with consistent leaf development. It adapts well to submersed aquariums and also performs exceptionally in paludariums and ripariums when grown emersed.

products.title: Anubias Petite White Marble
products.body_html:
Miniature leaves in white and pale cream, barely half an inch across. Anubias barteri var. nana 'Petite White Marble' is among the most heavily variegated plants in the hobby — and one of the least forgiving. A collector's plant, not a first Anubias.

What You'll Receive

  • 1 Bare-root Anubias Petite White Marble plant
  • Carefully selected and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®

Each plant is unique. Leaf coloration, marbling pattern, and size may vary naturally.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Petite White Marble Anubias
  • Scientific name — Anubias barteri var. nana 'Petite White Marble'
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to West Africa
  • Placement — Midground; attach to driftwood, stone or décor
  • Leaf size — Approximately 0.5-1 inch
  • Mature height — 2-4 inches
  • Growth rate — Very slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Low. Not medium, not bright — see the note below.
  • CO₂ — Not required, though stable CO₂ helps a plant with this little photosynthetic capacity.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5. Stability matters more than any specific value.
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte — attach the rhizome to hardscape and never bury it.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; grows emersed as well as submersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • White tissue does no work. The pale areas carry little or no chlorophyll, so the plant runs on whatever green is left — on a heavily marbled specimen that is very little. Everything follows from this: near-static growth, slow recovery from damage, and no capacity to shrug off a bad month.
  • Low light, always. Pale tissue burns where green tissue would be fine, and more light will not produce more marbling. Shade under driftwood or behind taller plants is the right position.
  • Algae is the real threat. A plant this slow cannot outgrow anything. Keep the tank balanced, keep the light down, and if algae does establish, do not scrub — the leaves are tiny and tear easily.
  • It can revert to green. Under stress the plant may push plain green leaves. Those leaves are healthier but they are not what you bought; trim them at the rhizome if you want the marbling to stay dominant.
  • Do not divide it early. At this growth rate a division may take a year to look like a plant again. Let it build a substantial rhizome first.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Anubias Care Guide.

Notes

Photos are for reference only. Marbling varies plant to plant, so the specimen you receive will not match the photograph. Growth is slow and survival depends heavily on proper care and placement. This plant is not recommended for beginners.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5, soft to moderately hard
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte — attach the rhizome to hardscape and never bury it.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; grows emersed as well as submersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division, plus plantlets from mature leaves

Grower's Notes

  • Scale is the reason to choose Mini. Full-size Java Fern Philippine reaches 8-14 inches and dominates a small tank. This one gives the same narrow waved leaf at a size that keeps a nano scape in proportion.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots may go into substrate; the green horizontal stem must stay in open water or it rots — the single most common way a Java Fern is killed.
  • Black spots on old leaves are baby plants, not disease. Java Fern reproduces by growing plantlets along the leaf margins. Leave a spotted leaf in place until each plantlet has roots and two or three leaves, then detach and attach it elsewhere. On a small plant this is how you build a group.
  • Keep the light modest. It grows slowly enough that strong lighting mostly feeds algae — and algae on a 2-inch leaf is far harder to clean off than on a large one.
  • Expect a change of leaf. We grow this emersed, so some arriving fronds will die back as it converts to submerged growth. As long as the rhizome stays firm and green, new leaves follow.
